Roya Publication No. 118
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

Nasrin is twenty-two and from the part of Tehran where the money never went. The job is in the part where it did: nanny to a six-year-old girl in a walled house on Fereshteh Street, in the north of the city, for three times what she made at the beauty salon. The old man who owns it looks at her once and then at the wall. The cook, Touran, has been there thirty years. The little girl takes her hand on the stairs.

Small wrong things. Touran cooks for one more than lives in the house. There is a photograph of three boys that nobody explains. And every night at eleven the pipes knock — four, a pause, two — and the child says it is the house saying goodnight.
The maids on the street have a name for the place. They have heard it for years. The owners have never once asked.

What Nasrin finds at the end of the back corridor has been there since 2004. What she decodes, one knock at a time, from the long conversation on Thursday nights, is older and stranger than a secret: it is the thing that has been holding the house up. And when a poor woman finds the holiest thing a rich family owns, she does what poor women do. She names a price.

A noir in four parts about the comfort money buys, the things poverty teaches, and what grows in a room when you leave a child in it for twenty-two years with a plate a day, four hundred books, and nobody to lie to.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book began with a film.

Parasite, the Korean film from 2019, is about a poor family who get into a rich house one lie at a time, and about what is already living in that house when they arrive. What stayed with me was not the plot but the shape: funny and then not; every person doing something reasonable and the sum a catastrophe; the rich not cruel and the poor not good; and a floor below the floor that nobody upstairs has ever thought to ask about. Most of all the man in the basement, down there for years, sending messages nobody reads, grateful for the light switch.

I wanted to write toward that man. Not copy him — the film has done him. I wanted to ask what he would actually be, after that long. Not a device; a person. What does a room make, if you give it a child and twenty years?

So this is a book about two kinds of life that share a wall. Upstairs is the comfort money buys: the trees, the quiet, the agreement not to notice things. Downstairs is the other kind: the plate at nine, the bus from Khazaneh [khah-zah-NEH], the price you learn to put on everything because somebody has always put one on you. The film taught me that these two lives are not opposites. They are the same house, each holding the other up, and under each is a thing it cannot look at, and the thing is usually a person.

Here that person is Zal [ZAHL], and he was built from two things. The first is what is actually known about children raised in isolation; the real cases are in the second interlude, and every strange thing he does has a precedent in somebody who lived. The second is a book — one book, on the table in the cellar, read more than two hundred times, the only account of people and what they do to each other that he has ever had. I am not going to name it here. Nasrin does not learn what it is until very late, and neither should you; when it comes, it is told plainly for anyone who has not read it. I will say only that I chose it because a boy with nothing else would not read it as a story. He would read it as instructions. And that the words are old enough to borrow, and I have borrowed several, and they are his now.

One more thing, said carefully. This is a book about a house with two kinds of life in it, and about the thing both kinds keep in the cellar — the thought that says plainly what the person upstairs will not: kept, or thrown away. Everyone in the house has it. Everyone in the street has it. I think everyone has it. The book is about what happens when a family builds a room for that thought and feeds it, and what it does when it is let out.

I should say plainly what is in this book, because it goes further than most on this list. There is a shelf of small skulls and the reader is told what they were. There is sex between a woman and a man who has never seen a body, written without romance. There is a child who died and a brother who feels nothing about it and says so. A woman dies on a mountain road and another dies in her bed, and the book does not tell you how much of either was arranged, because nobody in the house will ever ask. If you would rather not go down the stairs, this is the place to stop.

The Morse is real: H is four shorts and A is a short and a long, and ha — yes, the way you say it to the next room — is the shortest word in the code that means anything in Persian. I found that while writing, the way Nasrin finds it. The tap code of Hanoi is real, and the sign-offs. The arghavan [ar-ghah-VAHN] is, for the record, purple. Touran does not look.

I do not know whether Zal is to blame for anything. The old man made the decision; Touran kept him alive; his brother kept him company and kept him down; a street of servants heard the house knock for twenty years and never asked, because the owners never asked, and the owners never asked because nobody listens to pipes. He is what they made. Every one of them is a nicer person than he is. I have tried to write it so that both of those are true at once, because that is how it seemed to me, and because I think that is how it usually is.
Chew Z
I. THE BEST JOB
The wall came first. That is how it is with those houses. You see the wall before you see anything else, and the wall is the house telling you what it thinks of you.

This one was the colour of old bone and twice my height, with glass set into the top of it, green and brown, the bottoms of bottles broken off and pushed into the cement while it was wet. Somebody had done that by hand a long time ago. I stood on the pavement in my good shoes and looked up at the glass and thought: a person did that. A person knelt up there with a bucket of broken bottles and made sure.

Fereshteh [feh-resh-TEH] Street — the name means angel — runs along the slope in Elahieh [eh-lah-hee-YEH], which is the part of Tehran where the money went when it wanted trees and air. The streets curve up toward the mountain. There are no shops. You can walk for twenty minutes and see nobody except other women like me, in headscarves and sensible shoes, carrying the shopping of people whose cars cost more than our mothers’ houses. I had come on two buses and the whole length of the Metro from Khazaneh [khah-zah-NEH], which is the part of the city where the money never went at all, down below the railway where the air in summer tastes of the brick kilns, up to Tajrish [taj-REESH] at the top, where the line ends because the mountain starts, and the trip had taken two hours and ten minutes, and I had counted every one of them because that is what I do. I count. My mother says I was counting before I could talk.

There was a small door in the big gate, and a button, and a camera the size of my thumb. I pressed the button. Nothing happened for a long time. Then the small door opened by itself, with a sound like a lock giving up, and I went in.

The house was set back behind a garden that had been made to look wild and had cost a great deal to look that way. There was an arghavan [ar-ghah-VAHN] tree, bare, because it was January. There was a path of flat grey stones. There was a man standing at the top of the steps in a cardigan, and he was old, and he looked at me once, the whole of me, from the shoes up, and then he looked at the wall beside my head and kept looking at it while he spoke.
“You are the girl from the agency.”
“Yes, Agha.” Agha [ah-GHAH] — sir; what you call the man of a house.
“You have references.”
“Yes, Agha. Two.”

“Touran [too-RAHN] will see them.” He turned and went inside. He walked carefully, the way old men walk when they have decided not to use a stick. I never heard anyone call him by his name in all the time I was in that house. He was the Agha to Touran, Baba to his son, Baba-bozorg [bah-BAH boh-ZORG] — grandfather — to the little girl, and to me he was the old man, from the first minute, and I never thought of him as anything else.

Touran saw my references in the kitchen. She was a wide woman in her sixties with her hair pulled back so tight it lifted her eyebrows, and she read the two letters slowly, moving her lips, and then she folded them and put them in the pocket of her apron and did not give them back.
“You cook?”
“A little.”
“You don’t need to cook. I cook. You need to keep the child alive and quiet and clean, in that order. You can read?”
“Yes.”
“She likes to be read to. The last one couldn’t read properly. She would skip the long words.” Touran looked at me the way the old man had not — straight on, taking her time. “You’re small.”
“I’m strong.”
“That isn’t what I said.” But she nodded, and that was the interview, or I thought it was.
It was not. The interview was the stairs.

They sent me up to meet the child. The stairs were wide and dark wood and turned twice, and on the first landing there was a little girl sitting with her knees up, waiting, the way children wait when they have been told to wait and have decided to do it exactly. She was six. She had a drawing in her hand and the drawing was of a house, and the house had a face.
“Are you the new one?”
“I think so.”
“The last one was called Fatemeh [fah-teh-MEH]. She skipped the long words.”
“I heard.”
“What’s your name?”
“Nasrin.” Nas-REEN; it is a flower, a wild rose, and it is the most ordinary name in the city.
She considered it. “That’s short.”
“It’s all I’ve got.”

She stood up and took my hand. She did not ask; she took it, the way you take the rail of a bus. Her hand was warm and a little sticky and she held on hard. “I’m Yasmin,” she said, and she said it the way you say a thing that has been said to you many times, by many people, carefully: yas-MEEN. “I’ll show you where everything is. You’re not allowed in the back part. Nobody is. That’s where Touran lives.”
She took me up the second flight. At the top I looked down and the old man was standing in the hall below, looking up at us, at her hand in mine, and he had the face of a man watching a sum come out.

They offered me three times what I had made at the beauty salon. I said yes before Touran had finished saying the number. I am not proud of that. I am not ashamed of it either. You do not grow up where I grew up and stay proud when somebody says a number like that out loud.

A servant does not learn a house by its rooms. She learns it by its doors — which ones she may open, which ones she may knock on, which ones she must not be seen near. Nobody gives you the list. You learn it by the way people’s faces change.

The front door was not mine. I came and went by the side, through a gate in the wall that led into the kitchen garden and from there into the kitchen itself. The kitchen was Touran’s, which meant it was a kind of shrine: everything had its place, and the place was not up for discussion. The ground floor beyond the kitchen was the old man’s — a study with the door always shut, a sitting room with the curtains always half drawn, a dining room where he ate alone at the head of a table for twelve. I went in there to serve and to clear and did not linger.

The first floor was the son’s. His name was Babak [BAH-bak]. He was thirty and he was a widower, which I learned on the second day from Touran, who said it the way you say the weather. He had a bedroom and a bathroom and a study of his own, at the end of the corridor, over the laundry. The study door was shut when he was in it and shut when he was not. Yasmin’s room was on that floor too, and a room for me beside it, with a bed and a window and a lock that worked, which was more than I had at home.
The second floor was closed. Sheets on the furniture. Nobody went up.
And then there was the back.

The back was the part of the house that Yasmin had told me about on the stairs. You reached it through the kitchen, through a door beside the big refrigerator that I took at first for a pantry. It was not a pantry. It was a corridor, narrow, with a concrete floor instead of tile, and it ran away from the kitchen into the rear of the house where the light did not reach. Off it was the laundry — two machines, a sink, a drying rack, a smell of soap and damp — and past the laundry was Touran’s room, and past Touran’s room the corridor went on a little further and ended in a door.

“Storage,” Touran said, the first time I looked down there. She said it without looking up from the onions. “Old furniture. The khanom’s things. Nobody goes.” Khanom [khah-NOM] — the lady; the mistress of a house.
“The khanom?”
“The Agha’s wife. She died. Before your time.” She finished the onion. “A long time before.”
Yasmin had her own version. “Touran reads down there,” she told me, on the stairs, with great confidence. “At night. The same book. Baba says it’s a very long book.”

I did the laundry myself, from the first week, because Touran’s knees were bad and the machines were low. So I was in that corridor every day. I got to know the sound of it — the hum of the machines, the drip of the sink tap that would not quite close, the particular silence of the far end, where the door was. It was a thick silence, and it had a smell: esfand [es-FAND]. Everybody knows it — the wild rue seed that every house keeps in a jar and throws on the coals against the evil eye, that crackles and pops and gives off a sweet bitter smoke you carry round the rooms and the people. My mother did it every Thursday for my father. Here the smell lived at the end of the corridor and did not go away between Thursdays. I noticed it the way you notice a cold spot in a swimming pool. I noticed it and I did not go near it, because I had been in a house like this before, and in that house I had gone near something, and I had said what I saw, and I had been out on the pavement with my bag by the end of the afternoon with a reference that said I was unreliable.
I had learned. Or I thought I had.
Let me tell you about Touran, because she is the reason for everything, and because I loved her, and because she is dead now and nobody else is going to.

She had been in that house for thirty years. She had come as a young woman from a village near Hamedan [hah-meh-DAHN], in the west, that she never named, and she had cooked for the old man’s wife when the old man’s wife was young, and she had cooked for the children when there were children, and now she cooked for an old man who ate alone and a widower who ate standing up and a little girl who ate what she was told. She had a crooked ring finger that she said she had broken on a drawer. She had two bad knees that she said nothing about at all; you knew by the way she came down the back stairs, one step, both feet, the next step, both feet, with a hand on the wall. She wore the same grey cardigan every day over her apron and she had a radio on the windowsill that played old songs from before the revolution, the ones you cannot buy any more and everyone has — very quietly, all day, so that the kitchen always sounded like somebody else’s memory.

She ran that kitchen the way a mullah runs a mourning. Everything in order. Everything at its time. The old man’s coffee at seven, in the blue cup. Babak’s at seven-fifteen, black, in the car on his way out, in a paper cup she had ready by the side door. Yasmin’s tea at eight. Lunch at two. Dinner at eight-thirty. Nothing was ever late and nothing was ever asked for twice.
And every day, at nine at night, when the house had eaten and the dishes were done, she made one more plate.

On Thursdays she did one thing more. She took the little brass dish with the holes in the lid down from above the stove, and put three coals in it from the gas, and when they were red she threw a fistful of esfand on them from the jar and let it crackle, and carried the smoking dish through the door beside the refrigerator into the back, and I heard her go down the corridor with it, slowly, and come back without it. For the eye, she said, when she saw me looking. Thursday night is for the dead; you know that. The smoke went down the corridor and stayed there.
I noticed it on the third day. I notice things. It is not a virtue. It is a problem I have, like the counting.

The old man had eaten. Babak had eaten. Yasmin had eaten and was asleep. Touran had eaten standing at the counter, the way she always did, as if sitting down to food would be admitting something. And then she took a clean plate from the rack and put food on it — a good amount, more than she had eaten herself, rice and a ladle of khoresh [khoh-RESH] — the stew that goes on rice — and two pieces of chicken and a round of bread folded over — and she covered it with another plate turned upside down, and she set it on the end of the counter by the door to the back, and she went on wiping down the stove as though she had done nothing at all.
I did not say anything. I went up to bed.

The next night she did it again. And the next. Rice, stew, meat, a round of bread, the plate on top, the end of the counter. I was clearing up beside her and I kept my eyes on my hands. The fourth night, when I came down early for a glass of water at a quarter to one, the plate was gone and the counter was wiped.
She cooked for six in a house of five. Every night. For thirty years, I would learn later — though she had cooked for more, once, when there had been more.

I did not ask her. I want to be clear about that, because of everything that came afterwards, because people will want to know when I knew and what I did about it. I did not ask. I had been taught not to ask, by a woman in a house in Zafaraniyeh [zah-fah-rah-nee-YEH] — the rich district next to Fereshteh — who had put me out on the street for asking, and I had decided — the way you decide things when you are twenty-two and poor and have a mother with a bad roof — that I would never ask anything in a rich house again. Whatever that plate was for, it was Touran’s. It was none of mine.

That is what I told myself. It is also true that I was afraid. I did not know yet what I was afraid of. The house had not told me. But I had the feeling you get in the Metro when the man beside you has not moved for three stops and you have stopped being able to look anywhere but at your own hands.
There was a photograph in the upstairs hall, on the wall outside Babak’s study, at the height of a grown man’s eyes, which meant I had to look up at it.

Three boys. Two of them about the same size and one much smaller, with his arms around the neck of the middle one, laughing, his face pushed into the bigger boy’s shoulder. A garden behind them — this garden, I thought, the arghavan in flower, so it was spring. The bigger boys were squinting into the sun. The little one had his eyes shut. The frame was silver and somebody polished it; there were no fingerprints on the glass.
Nobody told me who they were. Yasmin, who told me everything, walked past it every day as if it were a window.

But I saw the old man stop there. I was coming out of Yasmin’s room with her laundry and he was coming along the corridor from the stairs, slowly, and he stopped in front of the photograph, and he lifted his hand and put two fingers on the glass, on the little one, on the laughing face with the eyes shut. He held them there. Then he took them away and went on to wherever he was going, and he had not seen me, or he had and it did not matter, because I was the help, and the help is furniture.
That night I looked at the photograph again, on my own. There was a fingerprint on the glass now. Two. Right over the small boy. The next morning they were gone.

So that was a thing that happened in that house: the old man touched the photograph, and somebody — Touran, I supposed — wiped it, and nobody said a word, and the house went on. I understood, then, the first rule of the place, though I could not have put it in words yet. Everybody in that house had agreed not to notice something. They had agreed so long ago that the agreement had become the walls.
There was another photograph, in Yasmin’s room, on the shelf beside her bed, where she could see it lying down. A young woman, dark hair, laughing, a baby on her hip. The baby was Yasmin.
“Who’s that?” I asked, the first night I put her to bed, because that was the kind of photograph you are allowed to ask about.

“Maman.” She said it without any weight at all. “She died in the car. I was two. I don’t remember her.” She turned over, as if that were the end of it, and then turned back. “Baba says she was funny. I think I’d remember if she was funny.”
“Not if you were two.”
“That’s what Touran says.” And she shut her eyes, and that was that.

Two photographs, then. A little boy with his eyes shut, and a young woman with a baby. Two dead people on two different floors. I did not put them together. There was no reason to. Rich families have their dead the same as anyone; they just have better frames.
The house knocked at eleven.

I heard it the first night and thought it was the pipes. Every old building in Tehran has pipes that knock. You turn off a tap and somewhere in the wall there is a sound like a fist. That is what it was, I decided, lying in my new bed in the dark with the window open to the cold and the smell of wet garden coming in. A pipe.
Four knocks. A pause. Two.

I heard it the second night at the same time and it was the same: four, a pause, two. Not a fist. Too neat for a fist. The sound came from below me and to the side, from the direction of the back of the house, and it came up through the floor the way sound comes up through water — soft, with the edges taken off.

The third night I was lying beside Yasmin because she had had a bad dream and wanted somebody there until she slept. It was a Thursday. Before the knock came there was something else, so faint I took it for a radio in another house: a stringed instrument, a few notes, slow, stopping and starting, from the end of our own corridor. A setar [seh-TAR] — the small long-necked lute with four strings that is played alone, in a room, with the nail of one finger, and sounds like somebody thinking. Four notes. Then nothing. Then the knock came. Four. A pause. Two. And Yasmin, with her eyes shut and her voice thick, said: “That’s the house saying goodnight.”

And a minute after it, something else — a long, uneven knocking from somewhere below, that stopped and was answered and went on — which I took for the pipes settling, because that was the night I wanted it to be.
I lay very still.
“Who told you that?”
“Baba.” She was almost gone. “It does it every night. It’s saying goodnight. You’re supposed to say it back.”
“Do you?”
“In my head.”

She slept. I did not. I lay there and listened to the house not knocking any more, and I counted — I could not help it — the seconds between the four and the two. One. Just one. Every night, one second. The same.

Here is a thing about me. I grew up in a building in Khazaneh with eleven families in it and walls you could hear a man think through. I know what a building sounds like when it is only a building. Pipes knock when water moves; they knock in a mess, in a hurry, they rattle and stop. They do not knock four times, wait one second, and knock twice, at eleven o’clock, every night, as if they had a watch.
Somebody was doing that.

I did not go and look. I want to be honest about that too. I lay in a child’s bed in a rich man’s house with her hot little hand on my arm and I thought: somebody is doing that, and everybody in this house knows it, and they have told the child it is the house saying goodnight, and the child believes them, and I am not going to be the one who asks. I am going to lie here, and I am going to say it back in my head, like she does.
Goodnight.
And I did. God help me, I did. I said it back in my head to whoever was knocking, and I went to sleep, and I slept fine.
On Fridays the maids of Fereshteh go to the park.

It is not a rule. Nobody tells you. You just find yourself there, on the first Friday afternoon of your first week, in your own manteau [man-TOH] — the long coat we wear outside — for once, on a bench by the fountain in the little park at the bottom of the hill, and there are the others — women in their own clothes, from Afghanistan and the villages of Lorestan [loh-res-TAHN], and from the far south of the city — eating ice cream out of paper cups and talking about their houses. Not their homes. Their houses. The ones they work in. Every woman in that park belonged, in the way that mattered that day, to a house.
They knew mine before I said the address.
“The bone wall,” said a woman from the house across the street, who had been there nine years. “With the glass on top.”
“Yes.”
“With Touran.”
“You know Touran?”

“Everybody knows Touran. Touran’s been there since God was a boy.” She licked her spoon. She had a way of looking at you sideways while she talked, as if checking who else was listening. “So you’ve heard it, then.”
“Heard what?”
She smiled. It was not an unkind smile. It was the smile you give a girl who has got a job that pays three times the beauty salon and has not yet worked out why.

“Khaneh-ye dar-zan [khah-NEH-yeh dar-ZAN],” she said. The house that knocks. “That’s what we call it. Everybody on the street. You can hear it from the back bedrooms in my house if the window’s open. Eleven o’clock. Been doing it for years.”
“Years?”

“Since before I came. Ashraf [ash-RAF] Khanom” — she tipped her head at a woman at the next bench, older, in a blue dress — “she was at the Sadeghi [sah-deh-GHEE] house two doors up for fifteen years, she says it was knocking when she started. Four and two. Every night.”
“What is it?”
The woman shrugged. “Pipes, Touran says.”
“It’s not pipes.”
“No.” She looked at me sideways. “It’s not pipes.”
“Then what —“

“Dokhtaram [dokh-tah-RAM],” she said — my daughter, the way older women say it to younger ones, kind and final — “do you know how long I’ve been across the street? Nine years. Do you know how many times the owners of my house have asked me what that sound is, in the night, that they can hear from their own bedroom with their own ears? Never. Not once. Nine years.” She finished her ice cream and set the cup down beside her on the bench. “The owners never ask. That’s the thing about that street. They never do. So we don’t either.”
I sat with that. The fountain went on. A child somewhere was crying about a balloon.

“There was one who asked,” the older woman in the blue dress said. Ashraf Khanom. She had not seemed to be listening. She was looking at the fountain. “A girl. At the bone wall. Ten years ago now. A maid, not a nanny — this was before the child. She asked Touran about it. Then she asked the son.”
“And?”

“And she was gone by the next Friday.” Ashraf Khanom turned and looked at me for the first time. Her face was quite calm. “With a good reference. Touran told us. A very good reference. She’s in Rasht [RASHT] now, I heard. Doing well.”
Nobody said anything for a while.

“Well,” said the woman from across the street, standing up, brushing off her skirt. “It’s a good house. Touran’s fair. The old man’s quiet. The son’s never there. The child’s sweet. You could do a lot worse, dokhtaram. We all could.” She looked down at me. “Just say goodnight back and go to sleep. That’s what the little one does, isn’t it? Say goodnight back. Eleven o’clock. That’s all it wants.”

She went. The others drifted after her. I sat on the bench until the light went and I had counted every stone in the rim of the fountain, twice, and the number was the same both times, which was something.
Thursday was different. I had known for two weeks that Thursday was different and had not let myself know it.

On Thursdays the knock at eleven was not four and two. It was four and two, and then, after a minute — after the house had settled, after I had said goodnight back in my head like a fool — it started again, and it did not stop. It went on. Long and short, long and short, in bursts and pauses, like rain starting and stopping on a tin roof, from below and to the side, from the back; and then, when it paused, something answered it. From above. From the end of the corridor on my own floor, from the direction of the study over the laundry where Babak shut himself in on Thursdays with a glass he did not drink from. Faint, through the wall. The same kind of sound. Long and short. And then the one below would start again.

It went on for an hour. Sometimes more. I lay in my bed and listened to two people talk in a language of knocking, one of them under the floor and one of them down the hall, and I did not understand a word of it and I understood everything that mattered: it was two. It was a conversation. It had been going on for years.
On the third Thursday I got up.

I do not know why that night and not the others. I have thought about it. I think it was the ice cream woman on the bench saying just say goodnight back, and the way she had said it, kind and tired, like a woman telling you how to live with a husband who hits. I think something in me, the part that counts, had added up the plate and the photograph and the fingerprints and the knock and the girl who went to Rasht with a good reference, and had got a number, and did not like it.
I went down the back stairs in my socks. The kitchen was dark except for the clock on the stove. The plate was not on the counter. It was ten past midnight.
The door beside the refrigerator was open a hand’s width.

I went through it into the corridor. Concrete under my feet, cold through the socks. The laundry machines were silent. Touran’s door was shut, but there was no line of light under it, and when I put my ear close I heard nothing — no radio, no breathing, nothing; she was not in there. The knocking had stopped some time ago. The thick silence at the end of the corridor was the only thing in the house that was awake.
The door at the end was not shut.

It was a plain wooden door with a plain brass handle and it stood open a few inches on darkness, and from the darkness came a smell — not bad, not what you would think; damp stone and candle wax and old paper, and under all of it esfand, thick, fifty-two Thursdays a year for twenty-two years of it with nowhere to go but down — and a faint moving light, yellow, low down, that came and went as if somebody were walking past it with a candle. And a voice. Touran’s. Low, the way you talk to someone in a hospital. I could not hear the words. And then another voice answered her, and that one I could hear, because it was closer to the door, and because it was clear, every word of it, in a Persian nobody speaks any more, the Persian of the old radio plays, careful and complete, every syllable finished:
“— then she is early. Tell her to come down. The stairs are steep; she should keep her hand on the wall.”
I had not made a sound. I was sure I had not made a sound.

Touran came to the door. She looked at me standing in the corridor in my socks with my hand against the wall where I had put it without deciding to, and her face did not change at all. It had the look of a woman who has been waiting a long time for a particular bus and has just seen it turn the corner.
“Well,” she said. “Come on, then. He’s right about the stairs.”

She went back in. The light moved. I stood for a moment longer in the cold, and then I went through the door, and found the top of a flight of stone steps going down into a yellow glow, and I put my hand on the wall, as I had been told, and I went down. At the bottom was a second door, a heavier one, standing open against the wall, and the room was through it.

The room at the bottom had been a wine cellar once. You could see where the racks had been. Now there were shelves — books, hundreds of them, in no order I could see — and a bed made with military tightness, and a table with a candle on it, and a bucket in the corner with a lid, and a square of grey high in the far wall where a vent let in what passed, down here, for light. It smelled of paper and stone and a man.

He was sitting on the edge of the bed with a book open on his knee — a thick one, swollen with damp, the cover gone and the spine held with tape, the pages the colour of tea — and he looked up at me when I reached the bottom step. He was twenty-eight years old — I knew that later; that night I could not have told you if he was twenty or forty. He was pale the way nothing above ground is pale, the colour of the inside of a shell. He was thin and very still and he had a long face with Babak’s bones in it, and the old man’s, and the little boy’s in the silver frame. His hair had been cut by somebody who loved him and could not see very well. His eyes were dark and quite calm and they did not look at my face. They looked, I understood much later, at my feet, and my hands, and the rise of my breathing, which were the things that told him anything.

“You are early,” he said, politely, in that old careful Persian. “Touran does not usually bring the plate until a quarter past. But it is all right. I have finished the chapter.” He closed the book, keeping his place with one finger. “You are the new one. Nasrin. The child says you do not skip the long words.”
I did not say anything. I could not have.
“That is good,” he said. “I do not either.” He laid his hand flat on the open page, the way you would on a cat, to keep it still. “There are a great many long words in this one.”

Behind me, Touran set the plate down on the table and lifted the top one off it, and the smell of rice and khoresh filled the stone room, and the man on the bed turned his head toward it the way a plant turns toward a window — and that was the moment, that small animal movement, when I understood that whatever was in this cellar had been in it for a very long time.
TAP CODE — I
The prisoners who talked through walls
A short note before the story goes on. This book is about two people who talk through a pipe. It has been done before, by real people, in worse rooms than a wine cellar. Here is how.

In 1965 an American pilot was shot down over North Vietnam and put in a prison the prisoners called the Hanoi Hilton. His name was Carlyle Harris; the others called him Smitty. He was kept alone. Everyone was kept alone. That was the point of the place: a man alone will break, and a man who can talk to another man will not.

Harris remembered something. An Air Force instructor had once shown him, almost as an aside, a code that prisoners had used in an earlier war. It was simple enough to learn in an afternoon and simple enough to send with a knuckle on a wall.
You write the alphabet in a square, five across and five down. Twenty-five boxes. The letter K is left out — you use C instead — so that twenty-six letters fit in twenty-five squares.
A B C D E F G H I J L M N O P Q R S T U V W X Y Z

To send a letter you tap twice. The first taps say which row. The second taps say which box along the row. So A is one tap, pause, one tap. The letter O is three taps — third row — pause, four taps — fourth box along. You do not need to remember dots and dashes. You only need to count.

Harris taught it to the next man through the wall, and that man taught the next, and inside a year every American in that prison could talk to the man in the next cell without a sound a guard could name. They tapped the news. They tapped jokes. One of them said afterwards that the building sounded like a den of woodpeckers. When a man was taken away for interrogation the others tapped to him when he came back, we are here, we are here, until he could answer. One of them, a navy commander called Stockdale, was held for eight years, about four of them alone, and tapped his way through them; he said the tapping carried everything a voice could — elation, sadness, humour, sarcasm. The men said afterwards that the code had kept them sane. They did not mean it as a figure of speech.

The tap code was not new even then. Russian prisoners under the tsars had used a square of their own a hundred years earlier; the revolutionaries learned it in prison and taught it to each other, and it is in their books. In every country that has built a wall between two people and told them not to speak, somebody has worked out how to knock.

The code in this book is not the tap code. It is Morse, which is older — made for the telegraph in the 1830s and 40s — and which uses shorts and longs instead of rows and columns. Morse is harder to learn and easier to send fast once you have learned it, and it is the one that was in a Pishahangi [peesh-ah-han-GEE] manual — the Iranian Scouts, before the revolution — in the 1970s, which is the only reason it matters here. The point is the same. The point is always the same.
A wall is only a wall until there is somebody on the other side of it. Then it is a telephone that has not been picked up yet.

The men in Hanoi had a sign-off. When the tapping was over and the guards were coming, the last thing one man sent to another was three letters. G.B.U. God bless you. Some pairs had their own — Stockdale and the man through his wall ended every night with S.T., sleep tight. So that whatever happened before morning, the last thing that had passed through the wall was that.

In the house in this book the sign-off is shorter still. Two letters, four knocks and two. It does not mean God bless. It means yes. But it is sent for the same reason, at the same hour, by two men who cannot see each other, and it has been sent every night for twenty years, and nobody above the floor has ever asked what it means.
II. THE ONE WHO KNOCKS
Touran told me at the kitchen table at one in the morning, because there was no point in not telling me now.

She made tea. Not for comfort — Touran did not do comfort — but because her hands needed something to do while she said it, and because a story like that goes down better with something hot. She put the cup in front of me and sat, which I had never seen her do, and she folded her hands on the table, the crooked finger on top, and she looked at the stove and not at me and she told it the way you tell a thing you have told yourself every night for twenty-two years and never once out loud.

“There were three boys,” she said. “You’ve seen the photograph. Babak, the oldest. Zal [ZAHL], two years younger — the khanom chose it, out of the old book of kings; it’s the one who was born with white hair and left out on the mountain, and a bird raised him. She said it was a strong name. The old man never liked it. And the little one. He was four.”
She did not say the little one’s name. She never did, in all the time I knew her. He was the little one, the way the old man was the Agha, as if a name would have made him too heavy to carry.

“It was April. 2004. The arghavan was out. The khanom — the Agha’s wife — she was alive then, she was downstairs, she had people for lunch. I was in the kitchen. The boys were on the roof. There’s a terrace up there, you haven’t seen it, nobody goes now. They played up there. There was a wall, a low wall, and I’d told the khanom a hundred times it was too low for the little one and she said boys have to learn.” Touran’s hands did not move. “The two big ones were up there with him. Nobody else. And he went over.”
I said nothing. The tea steamed between us.

“I heard the khanom before I heard anything else. Then I was in the garden and the little one was on the stones and the Agha was there and he had his hand on the boy’s chest like he could hold him in. And Babak came down the stairs white as a plate. And then Zal came down behind him, and he was — “ She stopped. For the first time her voice moved. “He was six. He had a face on him I can’t describe to you. Not crying. Like a boy who’d been told something he didn’t understand yet. And the Agha looked up at the two of them on the steps, and Babak said — “
She stopped again.
“Babak said, Zal pushed him.”
The clock on the stove ticked. Somewhere in the walls a pipe settled, an ordinary sound.

“And Zal didn’t say anything. He looked at his brother and he looked at his father and he didn’t say a word. Six years old. He just stood there and let it be true.” Touran unfolded her hands and put them flat on the table. “And the Agha made a decision. Right there. On the stones with his hand on his dead son’s chest. I watched him make it. I’ve never seen a man think so fast in my life.

“No police. No doctor — the little one was gone, there was nothing a doctor could do except write things down. The khanom’s people were sent home; she said the boy had a fever. That night the Agha drove to Nowshahr [now-SHAHR] with the little one wrapped in the back of the car. They have a house there, on the water. And a week later it was in the papers — a tragedy, two children of a good family drowned at Nowshahr, swept off the breakwater in the spring sea, the bodies not recovered. Two. The little one. And Zal.”
“But — “

“There is a grave for each of them in the Behesht-e Zahra [beh-HESHT-eh zah-RAH]. The big cemetery in the south, where the whole city goes. I’ve seen them. White stone. Washed every year on the last Thursday, by a man he pays.” She looked at me then, straight on, the way she had the first day. “And Zal has been down those stairs since that night. The Agha took him down himself. He said, You will stay here where you can’t hurt anyone else, and Touran will feed you, and that is more than you deserve. And he gave me an envelope the first of every month from then on, in cash, on top of my wage. And I took it. And I fed him.”
“For twenty-two years.”

“For twenty-two years.” She picked up her cup for the first time and drank, and set it down. “He is a good boy. He has always been a good boy. Whatever happened on that roof, he was six, and he has never been anything but good to me.”
I looked at her hands on the table, and at the crooked finger, and she saw me look, and she said, “A drawer,” and I nodded, and we both let that be true as well.
I went down alone the next night.

Touran did not stop me. She did not help me either. She put the plate on the end of the counter at nine as she always did, and at a quarter past midnight she went to bed with her door shut and her radio off, and the plate was still there, and the door beside the refrigerator was open a hand’s width, and I understood that this was how she had decided to do it. She would not take me down. She would not keep me out. She would leave the door open and go to sleep and let the house decide.
I took the plate.

Before she went to bed, Touran gave me tea. She always did, after that; it was part of going down. Black, in a glass, very sweet, and in the bottom of the glass a pinch of something that did not dissolve — small dark seeds, bitter under the sugar. Esfand. “For the eye,” she said, “since you’re going near him.” My mother had done the same before my father’s night shifts. I drank it. I always drank it.
I went down the stone stairs with my hand on the wall.

He was at the table this time, with the candle, and a book, and he did not look up until I had put the plate down and lifted the cover, and then he looked at the food and not at me, and he said, “Thank you,” in that voice from an old radio, and he began to eat. He ate carefully. He ate everything, in order — rice, then the stew, then the meat, the bread last, wiping the plate — and when he had finished he set the fork down parallel to the knife and pushed the plate an exact distance away from him, and only then did he look in my direction.

Not at my face. I noticed that the second night as I had the first. His eyes went to my hands, my feet, the middle of me. He looked at my face the way you look at a page in a language you don’t read — briefly, politely, without expecting anything from it.
“You came back,” he said. “Touran said you might not. She said you had a look.”
“What look?”
“The look of someone adding things up.” He said it without any weight. “She said the last one who had that look went to Rasht. I do not know where that is. It is not in any of my books.”
“It’s north. About three hours.”
“North,” he said, as if filing it. “Thank you.”

I looked at the room, because I could not keep looking at him. The shelves went up to the ceiling on three walls — books, as I had seen the first night, but now I saw that they were not in no order; they were in an order I did not know, by size, or by colour, or by something else. One book was not on the shelves at all. It lay on the table beside the candle, the swollen one with no cover, squared to the table’s edge in reach of his right hand, and I understood from where it lay that it lived there. The bed was made so tight you could have bounced a coin. The floor was swept. The candle sat in a saucer in the exact centre of the table. High on the fourth wall, where the racks had been, a square of darker grey was the vent, and under it a row of small things I could not make out. In the corner, a bucket with a wooden lid.
“What colour is the car?” he said.
“What?”

“Babak’s car. He has had it four years. I know the sound of it very well, going out and coming back, and the sound the gate makes for it. Touran says it is grey, but she said the last one was grey, and I do not think she looks. What colour is it?”
“It’s — blue. Dark blue.”
“Blue.” He closed his eyes for a moment. I would learn that he did this when he was putting something away. “Dark blue. Thank you. That is better than grey.”
I looked at the book on the table. He saw me look; he saw everything.
“You may,” he said.

I turned it toward me. The cover was gone and the title page with it; the first page that was left began in the middle of a sentence, in a Persian older than anyone alive, on paper soft as cloth. A child had written a name inside in pencil and someone had rubbed it out. I did not know what it was. I did not ask. He did not say.

“It came down in the first box,” he said. “With a Quran and a dictionary and some old things of Babak’s. I could not read it for two years; the words were too long. Then I could. I have read it two hundred and eleven times. The Quran forty. The others once or twice.” He took it back from me gently and squared it to the table’s edge. “It is about a man. What he becomes. What he does afterwards. It is the best book that has been written. I have read all the others, so I would know. It is the only account of people and what they do that I have ever had.”

That was how he talked. I had taken it for the radio. It was not the radio. It was that book, read two hundred and eleven times in a Persian from another century — every sentence finished, every word in its coat — and it was, though I did not understand this for a long time, the only account of people and what they do that he had ever had.
And then he stood up, and went to the corner, and lifted the lid of the bucket, and turned his back to me, and used it — standing, the way men do — and went on talking over his shoulder while he did.

“You are from Khazaneh. Touran told me. I know it from the radio; there was a woman on a programme once who came from there, she said the canal comes up into the streets in the spring. Does it still come up?”

I had turned to the wall. I heard the sound of it, and the lid go back on, and his feet on the swept floor coming back to the table, and I understood that nothing had happened as far as he was concerned. He had needed the bucket and he had used it and he had gone on with the conversation, because nobody had ever taught him that this was a thing you stopped a conversation for, and there had been nobody down here to learn it from. For twenty-two years the only other person in this room had been a woman who changed that bucket every morning and had long since stopped seeing it.
“Yes,” I said to the wall. “It still comes up.”
“I thought it might,” he said, sitting down. “Things like that do not usually stop.”
The row of small things under the vent was skulls.
I did not understand what I was looking at the third night, and then I did, and I stood there with the plate in my hands and could not put it down.

They were on a narrow shelf of their own, a plank set into the stone, at the height of his head when he was sitting. Eleven of them. They were in a row, by size, the smallest on the left — a thing the size of a thumbnail — and then larger, and larger, delicate things with long teeth, and then one with a short hooked beak that I knew for a bird, and then at the right-hand end one that was not like the others at all. It was the size of my fist. It had eye sockets I could have put my fingers in, and a long jaw, and the teeth were still in it.
He saw me looking. He saw everything; I had learned that already. Not with his eyes — with whatever he used instead.

“The shelf,” he said. “Touran does not like it either. She asked me to keep them in a box and I said no.” He got up and came and stood beside me and looked at them with me, like a man showing a visitor his garden. “Touran comes once a day. In the beginning, when I was small, she came twice, but the Agha found out and stopped it. Once a day. One plate. It is a good plate, she is generous, but it is once.” He pointed, not touching. “Everything else that comes into this room is food. That is a rule I made when I was eight. It is a good rule. It has kept me alive.”
“These are — “

“Rats, those. They come in under the door; there is a gap, you can see it, Touran has asked for it to be fixed and the Agha does not send anyone down here. One learns to be quick. Those two are mice, which are not worth the trouble but one does not say no. That one — “ the beak — “came down the air shaft in 2011. A pigeon. It was alive when it arrived. It was the best thing I have ever eaten.” He said this simply. “And that one.”
The one on the end. The one with the teeth.

“A cat,” he said. “In 2017. Somebody’s, I think; it had a collar, I have it in the drawer. It came in under the door after a rat and could not find the way out again, in the fortnight Touran was in the hospital with her knees and a niece of hers left the plate at the top of the stairs without coming down, and it was down here with me for two days, and I fed it from my plate, and then I understood that it was not going to be found and that Touran would not be allowed to take it up, and that I had not had meat that was not chicken in ten years.” He looked at the skull. He had no expression on his face that I could read, but then, I could not read his face at all. “It was harder than the pigeon. Not the doing of it. The deciding. I was fond of it.”
I put the plate down on the table. My hands did it; I was not there.

“I have a question,” he said. “I have wanted to ask someone for a long time and Touran will not discuss it. You have been outside. You have seen both.” He turned toward me. “What is the difference between a cat and a chicken? Apart from the sound.”
And when I did not answer: “In the book a man eats what he is given and is grateful. It is the first thing he learns. I did not have to be taught it. I had the book.”

I went up the stairs. I made it to the laundry sink. I was sick, quietly, with the tap running, and then I rinsed the sink and rinsed my mouth and stood there with my hands on the cold edge of it in the dark.

And then I went back down. The next night. I want that understood. I went back down the next night with the plate, and the night after, and he never asked me why I had left in the middle of his question, and I never answered it, and the skulls stayed on their shelf, by size, and after a week I stopped seeing them, the way Touran had stopped seeing the bucket.
That is the thing nobody tells you about a house like that. It does not make you do anything. It just waits until you have stopped seeing.
He told me about the door himself. Not the one at the top of the stairs. The other one.

It was perhaps the second week. I had started staying after the plate was finished, sitting on the floor with my back against the shelves because there was only the one chair and he would not take the bed while I was there. He said it was not correct. He had got correct from a book — I never found out which — and he used it the way other people use God.
I had asked him how. That was all. How he had done it. Twenty-two years in a room the size of my mother’s kitchen with a bucket and a candle and a plate a day.
He thought about it for a while. He always did; he never answered anything fast.
“You know the door at the bottom of the stairs,” he said. “This one. It has a bolt. On this side. Did you see?”
I had. I had looked at it every night going out. A heavy iron bolt, old, on the inside of the cellar’s own door, where a man who wanted to keep people out would put it. It had never once been shot.

“The Agha put it there. In the first year. I think he thought that if I could lock myself in, I would feel safer, and if I felt safer I would be quieter. He was not wrong. I was a very quiet child.” He turned the book over on his knee. “But I understood, when I was nine or so, that the bolt on the door was not the one that mattered. There was a door inside me as well, and it had no bolt at all, and things were coming through it all the time that I could not have. The sky. I remembered the sky; I was six, I had seen it every day of my life. My mother. Being carried. The feel of grass. Being looked at — do you know that feeling? Being in a room with people who can see you?” He said it as if asking about a place I had been. “I could not have any of those things, and they kept coming through the door, and every time they came through I had to spend the rest of the day getting them back out again, and I was not getting any reading done.

“The book taught me that a man who keeps wanting a thing he cannot have is a man who dies of it. It says so, more or less, on a page I could find for you in the dark. So I made a second door. Inside. And I put a bolt on it, on my side, the same as the one upstairs. And I put the sky behind it, and my mother, and the grass, and being looked at, and being anybody. And I shot the bolt.” He looked at the candle. “It took about a year. It was the hardest thing I have done. Harder than the cat. But I have not had to do it twice. It has stayed shut.”
“You never — want to open it?”
“Wanting is on the other side,” he said. “That is the point of the door.”
I did not say anything for a long time. Then I said the stupidest thing I have ever said in my life.
“I’m sorry.”
He looked, for a moment, almost puzzled. “Why?”
“Because — “ I did not know how to say it to him. “Because of what they did. Because you’re here. Because it isn’t fair.”

“Fair,” he said. He said it the way he had said Rasht. “There is a line in the book. The man says it at the very end, when he has done everything he came to do. He says that there is no such thing as a happy man or a wretched one; there is only one state set beside another, and the setting beside is all there is. You would have to show me the other thing, for fair. The thing this is being compared to. I have only ever had this.” He opened the book again. “There were three of us on that roof. One is dead. One is upstairs with a glass he does not drink from, and I hear him some nights, through the pipe, when it is not Thursday and nobody has knocked, just walking, up and down, up and down. And one is here, with a plate every day and four hundred books and nobody to lie to.” He found his place. “I was kept. The little one was thrown away. I have thought about it a great deal, and I do not think I am the one you should be sorry for.”
He meant it. That was the thing I lay awake with afterwards, up in my bed down the corridor from the study. He meant every word of it, and he was wrong, and I could not have told you where.
He told me about Touran’s finger himself too. I had not asked. I had stopped asking him things by then; he gave them to you anyway, when he judged it was time, the way he gave you the skulls.
“She has told you it was a drawer,” he said.
“Yes.”

“It was me. I was nineteen. She was moving the shelf — that one, by the bed — because she thought the damp was getting at it, and I had not asked her to, and I took her wrist to stop her and I did not know how hard.” He said it without any change in his voice. “I heard it go. She did not cry out. She went upstairs and I did not see her for two days and a niece of Touran’s left the plate at the top of the stairs, as she had once before, and did not come down. When she came back the finger was strapped and she did not mention it and neither did I.”
“You didn’t say sorry.”

“I did not have anything to say it with.” He looked at me — at my hands, as always. “I understand that there is a thing people have. I have read about it. It is in all the books, people are forever doing it, falling on their knees. I think it is made of being looked at. You do a thing in front of someone and you see their face change and the thing that happens in you then, that is the material. I was last looked at when I was six.” He turned back to the candle. “I bit her, also. When I was nine. The first year of the knocking. She reached for the manual, the Scout book, to see what I was doing with it, and I thought she would take it, and I bit her hand to the bone. I am telling you so that you know. She has a mark. She will tell you it was a dog.”

I sat with my back against the shelves and I thought about the woman upstairs with her two bad knees and her crooked finger and her radio and her plate, every night for twenty-two years, for a boy who had bitten her to the bone and broken her finger and did not have anything to be sorry with.
And then the stairs creaked.

He was up before I heard it — or I was; I remember a knuckle on the iron of the pipe that came down the wall beside the vent, and I do not remember anyone crossing the room — and the knuckle knocked. Three times. Not the eleven o’clock four. Softer, and quicker, and without the two after.
Touran’s voice came down from the dark at the top. “Jigar? I heard you. Is she still there?”

Jigar [jee-GAR]. It means liver, and it is what you call a child you would give your own for. She had called him that since the night he went down, she told me later, because at six he had been too small for his name.
“She is here,” he called up. “Mind the fourth step. It is damp tonight.”
Her feet came down, one step, both feet, the next step, both feet, a hand on the wall.

“He does that,” she said to me, at the bottom, a little out of breath. “Since my knees went. So I don’t have to call down and wake the house. Three knocks when he hears me on the stairs and I know he’s heard and I can take my time.” She set a folded blanket on the end of the bed. “The nights are cold. You’ll catch your death down here, girl, sitting on stone.”
He had already gone back to his chair and his book. He did not look up. “Thank you, Touran.”
“Eat your orange,” she said, and went back up, one step at a time, and he waited until the top step had creaked and the door had settled before he turned a page.
Both things were true. I keep saying that. I do not know any other way to say it.
“The knocking,” I said. “At eleven.”
It was perhaps the third week. I had earned it, I thought. I had sat on his floor for twenty nights and not been sick again.
“Yes.”
“Four and two. Every night.”
“Yes.”
“What is it?”

He got up and took a book down from the shelf by the bed — not from the rows; from a place of its own, lying flat on top, where a hand could find it in the dark. It was small and soft-backed and falling apart, the cover gone, the pages the colour of tea. He opened it to a place it opened to by itself and held it out to me across the candle.
A table. Two columns. Letters down one side and, beside each letter, a little row of dots and dashes.

“When I was nine I heard the pipe knock,” he said, “and I thought: that is a wall, and there is someone on the other side of it. I needed a way to speak through it, and this came down the stairs the same month.” He opened it. “It is called Morse. A man called Morse made it, for the telegraph, which is a wire that carries clicks. Every letter is a pattern of short and long. A short is a dot, a long is a dash. You can send it with anything — a light, a wire, a finger on a pipe. The book is for boys. Scouts. It came down with a box of other things when I was nine. I think it was Babak’s; it has a name scratched out inside the cover.”
I looked at the table. I looked at the row of symbols against the letters and I thought of the four and the two, every night, one second between.

“Four short,” he said, “is H. A short and a long is A. H. A.” He took the book back. “Ha. Yes — the way you say it to someone in the next room when you cannot be bothered with baleh [BAH-leh], the polite one. That is all it is. At eleven I knock yes on the pipe, and the house knocks yes back, and we both know that the other is still here, and we go to sleep.”
“The house.”
“The house.”
“Who answers you?”
He put the book back in its place on top of the shelf, exactly where it had been, and sat down.

“The house,” he said again, pleasantly, and opened his novel. And I understood that he was lying to me, and that he knew I knew, and that he was letting me not believe him for as long as I wanted — the way you let a child go on thinking the moon follows the car.
Goodnight, I had said back, in my head, every night for a month. Not goodnight. Yes. I had been saying yes.

I am going to tell this part plainly because there is no other honest way to tell it, and because people will want to make it into something it was not — a love story, or a horror story — and it was neither. It was a thing that happened between a woman who had never been looked at properly and a man who had never seen a body, in a room under a house, and I do not fully understand it, and I am the one it happened to.

It began with my wrist. I should say that it was a Thursday, and that the smoke was in the room, and the setar had been going through the pipe for an hour, and the tea was in me; I say it not as an excuse but because it is true, and because afterwards I could never decide how much of what I felt was mine.

I had stayed late. The candle was low. I was on the floor with my back against the shelves and I had said something — I do not remember what — and he had got up from the chair and come across the room and crouched in front of me and taken my wrist in his hand, the way you take a cup, and put two fingers on the inside of it, where the pulse is.
“May I,” he said. After, not before.
I did not pull away. I should say that I was afraid, and I was, but not of him; I was afraid of the thing I could feel myself about to allow.

“Touran’s is slow,” he said. He was not looking at my face. He was looking at his fingers on my wrist with his whole attention, the way he looked at the plate. “Sixty, sixty-two. It has been slow for years. Yours is a hundred and four.” He counted silently. I saw his lips move. “A hundred and six now. Why?”
“You know why.”
“I do not,” he said. “That is why I am asking.”
Here is what I will say about the weeks that followed, and then I will stop.

He had never seen another body. Not since he was six, and a six-year-old does not see bodies, he sees people. He approached mine the way I had watched him approach the pigeon — in the telling, I mean; I was not there for the pigeon — with complete attention and no shame and no tenderness. Not cruelty. Tenderness is a thing you learn from being handled gently, and he had last been handled gently at six, and what was left in him in place of it was interest. He asked questions. During. What was this for. Why did I do that with my breath. Whether this was the same for everyone or only for me. He noted sounds. He said, once, that is the sound Babak’s wife made, through the ceiling, the year before she died — I always wondered what it was, and I nearly left and did not.

He did not know that he was supposed to stop doing what he was doing when I came down the stairs. The first time, I stood at the bottom step with the plate and he was on the bed and he finished — not hurriedly, not slowly, the way you finish a sentence — and sat up and said, “You are early again,” and I understood that nobody had ever told him this was a thing done privately because there had never been a private and a public in this room, only the room.
And I kept going down.

I have asked myself why for a long time. I will give you the answers I have, and none of them is the whole one. Because the money was good and he was part of the money. Because I was twenty-two and nobody in my life had ever paid me the kind of attention he paid a pulse. Because it was the most alive I had ever felt in my body and I had not known until then that I had not been feeling alive. Because I pitied him. Because I did not pity him at all, and that was a relief, after the pity. Because he was beautiful, in the way a thing is beautiful that has been made by only one force for a very long time, like a stone in a river.
Because he never once looked at my face, and I had been waiting all my life for somebody to stop looking at my face.
All of those. None of them. I went down, and I did not know what I had let touch me, and I knew exactly what I had let touch me, and I went down again.

I have to stop the story here and tell you about the smoke, because everything I did after this I did inside it, and if I do not tell you what it was like you will think I was a different kind of person than I am. I was not drunk. I was not dreaming. I was something I did not have a word for then and have only a poor one for now, and I will go slowly, because it went slowly.

It was the first Thursday I stayed in the laundry instead of going down. A quarter to eleven. The tea was in me — Touran’s black tea with the sugar and the seeds in the bottom, which I had drunk every night for weeks now without thinking, the way you take what a mother hands you. I sat on the concrete between the two machines with Yasmin’s exercise book on my knee and the pencil in my hand and my back against the warm enamel, and I waited for the knocking, and before the knocking came the other things.

The smoke came first. Touran had gone past the door with the brass dish, slowly, one foot and then the other on the concrete of the corridor, and the esfand was crackling on the coals, and I heard her set it down at the head of the stairs and come back without it. Smoke in a corridor does not rise. It finds the floor and moves along it like water looking for the lowest place. It came under the laundry door in a flat grey sheet and spread across the concrete and reached me and climbed me, and the smell of it was the smell of every Thursday of my childhood, my mother waving the dish around my father’s head before his night shift at the brick kilns, saying the words, let the eye of the envious burst — and I breathed it, and went on breathing it, and did not open the door, because it had never occurred to anyone in my life that the smoke was anything but a blessing.

Then the setar. From above, down the iron pipe that came out of the ceiling beside me and went down into the floor. Four strings and the nail of one finger, so quiet that if the machines had been running I would not have heard it. A few notes. A pause. The same few notes again, with one of them changed. A pause. I put my hand flat on the pipe to feel it, and the pipe was warm, which it had never been, and the notes came up into my palm as well as into my ears.
And then the room began to change, and I am going to tell you exactly how, because the how is the only part of it I am sure of.

The hum of the machines — they were not running, but a house hums; a refrigerator, a transformer somewhere, the city itself — stopped being a hum and became a note. One note, low, steady, under everything, the way the ground is under everything. And the setar was playing on top of that note, and had been all along, and I had not been able to hear it before. The corridor outside the door got longer. I could not see it; I knew it. The laundry got taller. The pipe under my hand was not iron any more, or it was iron and also a thing that went down through the floor and up through the ceiling and did not stop at either, and I was holding on to it the way you hold the rail on a bus that is going somewhere you have not been.

When the setar stopped, the line of it went on. That is the thing I most want you to understand. The man upstairs lifted his nail from the string and the sound went on inside me, the same few notes, turning over, as if the music had been in me all along and he had only been playing what was already there. And in the dark behind my eyes — my eyes were open; I could see the machine, the sink, the door; but behind them, in the place you see with your eyes shut — there was a pattern, small, repeating, like the holes in the lid of the brass dish, like the squares of the exercise book, like the stones in the rim of the fountain I had counted twice. I was not frightened. I was clear. That is the only word I have. Clear, and far from myself, and listening with my whole skin.

And in that clearness I understood something about the house, and then about the street, and then about myself, and I will put it as plainly as I can, because I have had a long time to find the words and these are the best ones.

Everyone I had ever met had been made. By a mother, a street, a school, a language, a God, a country. You could see the making on them like a tailor’s chalk. The old man had been made by money and by the year he was born. Touran had been made by a village and thirty years of somebody else’s kitchen. Babak had been made by this house. I had been made by Khazaneh and by counting. Yasmin was being made in front of me, day by day, with every sorry she was taught to say. That was what a person was, I had always thought: the thing the making made.

But under the making there was something else. I felt it that night the way you feel a current under a boat — not see it, feel it, in the way the boat moves against what your hands are doing. There was a part of every one of us that nobody had made. It had been there before the mother and the street and the God, and it did not speak their language, and it did not care what they wanted, and it had never once in its life been allowed to say anything out loud. It was the part that priced things. It was the part that knew who was kept and who was thrown away before anyone had decided. It was the part of my mother that had looked at my father, some nights, with a look that had nothing to do with love, and the part of the old man that had made his decision on the stones with his hand on his dead son’s chest before his grief had even arrived. It was the same part in all of them. In the rich house and the poor one. In the woman on the bench in the park who said the owners never ask and the owner who did not ask. It was not the part of us that was bad. It was the part of us that was there, under everything, like the note under the setar, like the ground under the house, and all the making in the world was only a floor laid over it so that we could walk around on top of it and not look down.

And I understood that the house had a floor like that too. And that the whole house — the old man, Touran, Babak, the little girl, the street — had agreed not to look at what was under it, the way you agree not to look at the thing under yourself. And that I had been looking at it for a month, every night, with a plate in my hands.

I did not think he is that. I want to be exact. I was not thinking in those words. I was feeling, with my whole clear skin, that the thing under the floor of the house and the thing under the floor of me were one thing, and that the smoke had not put it there. The smoke had only turned the lights on in the room where it had always been.

That is what I have to tell you about the esfand, and the setar, and the Thursdays. People will want it to be a drug, and it was, in the way that water is a drug to someone who has never seen their own face. It did not give me anything. It took away the floor for an hour, and let me look down, and what I saw was not a stranger. My mother would have said the eye was off me. I think the eye was finally on.
The knocking began inside that. Four, and two. Ha. And then the long runs. And I picked up the pencil, and I began.
The exercise book was Yasmin’s. A school one, squared paper, a cartoon dog on the cover. She had three and never used the third. I took it.
That first Thursday on the laundry floor, inside the clearness, I heard the whole hour and wrote almost none of it.
Four and two. Ha. And then, a minute later, from above, from the end of the corridor on my own floor — four and two. Ha.
And then the long knocking began.

I had thought I would write down dots and dashes. I could not. It was too fast. It came in runs — knock knock knock, pause, knock, long pause, knock-knock — and by the time I had decided whether a knock was short or long the next three had gone past. I filled a page with marks that meant nothing. I tore it out. I started again, and this time I did not try to tell short from long; I just made a mark for every knock and a space for every pause, and let the shape of it go onto the paper however it fell.

It went on for fifty minutes. Then it stopped — a pause longer than the others — and from above came a short run, and from below a shorter one, and then nothing, and the house settled, and I sat between the machines with six pages of pencil marks and my hand cramped shut, and the smoke gone thin, and the note the machines had been playing gone back to being a hum, and I was sick in the laundry sink, quietly, the way you are after esfand tea, and rinsed it, and went up.
The next Thursday I did it again. And the one after.

I am not clever. I want to say that. I am not one of those girls in the films who looks at a page of marks and sees the pattern. I am a girl who counts. So I counted. I counted which runs came most often. I counted how long the pauses were between runs and found that there were two kinds, a short kind and a longer kind, and I guessed — I did not know, I guessed — that the short kind was between letters and the longer kind was between words. And I took the Scout book down from its place on the top of the shelf one afternoon when he was asleep, because he slept in the afternoons with the vent at its greyest, and I copied the table into the back of the exercise book, and I put the Scout book back to a finger’s width, and I knew he would know anyway, and I did it.
And then I sat in the laundry, in the daytime, with the washing going, and I went through three Thursdays of marks with the table, one letter at a time.

Most of it was nothing. I had got the shorts and longs wrong, or missed knocks, or the pauses had fooled me. But some runs came again and again, the same shape, and the shape of one of them was seven letters long, and when I had worked it through the table — twice, three times, with my finger on the paper and my lips moving like Touran reading my references — it said:
B A R A D A R
Brother.

I sat on the laundry floor with the machine going round beside me and the exercise book open on my knees for a long time. I did not cry. I do not know what I did. I think I just sat there and let it be true, the way he had let it be true on the steps when he was six.
After the first word it went faster. That is how it is with anything — the first word costs you everything and the second one is nearly free.

I got better at hearing the shorts from the longs. I got better at the pauses. I began to take down whole runs cleanly and to work them through the table the next morning at the kitchen table with the exercise book open inside Touran’s big cookbook, so that anyone coming in would see a girl studying a recipe. Touran saw. Touran, who could not read Morse and could not have told you what a telegraph was, looked at the cookbook and at my face and went on with the onions.
The second word was a name.
Y A S M I N

I got it on a Tuesday morning from the marks of the Thursday before, and I had to put the pencil down. The letters had thrown me. The table in the manual was the foreign alphabet — the Scouts used the international one, the same as the English — and the brothers spelled Persian in it the way everyone spells Persian on a telephone, by the sound. I had learned those letters for two years at school and read them the way you read a shop sign. Y A S M I N meant nothing to me on the page until I said it out loud and heard it.
He was talking about her. Under the floor, to the house, every Thursday, about the little girl I put to bed.

The third word was H A N O O Z. Hanooz [hah-NOOZ]. Still. I got that one and a few around it — INJA, here; KHOOB, well; NA, no — and a run that I worked and reworked and that would not come out as anything, and that I understood later was his laugh, if that is what you call it on a pipe: a run of shorts with no pattern, just a sound a man makes.
And then one night in the laundry, taking down the marks, I understood something that I should have understood weeks before, that a girl who counts should have had on the first night.

The sound from below came up through the concrete between the machines. I had always known that. The sound from above — the answer — did not come from across the corridor, or from the kitchen, or from anywhere in the back. It came down. Down the same pipe. From directly overhead. I put my hand flat on the iron where it went up into the ceiling and I felt it, under my palm, the faint knock of an answer, coming down from the room above the laundry.
The study. The end of the corridor on my own floor. Babak’s study, where he shut himself in on Thursdays with a glass he did not drink from.

It was not the house. It had never been the house. For twenty years, every Thursday, for an hour, the man under the floor had been talking to the man above it — to his brother, who had said Zal pushed him on the steps when he was eight and had been answering the pipe since he was eleven — and the whole street had heard them and called it the house, and the little girl between them said goodnight to it in her head.

I took down the last run of that Thursday with my hand shaking so that I was not sure of it. I worked it the next morning in the cookbook. It was from below. It was the first whole sentence I ever got clean, start to finish, and it was a question, and it was not for me.
E M R O O Z C H I K E S H I D ?
Emrooz chi keshid [em-ROOZ chee keh-SHEED].
What did she draw today?
TAP CODE — II
The ones who were kept

Another note before the story goes on. You have met him now. You have seen the shelf and the bucket and the door he says he built inside himself. You will want to know if a person can really become that. Here is what is known.

Nobody has ever done to a child exactly what was done to the boy in this book, and then written it down. But people have come close, by accident and on purpose, and doctors and scientists have studied what came out. The boy is made from what they found. Here it is, in order, in plain words.

Language has a door, and the door closes. In 1970 a girl of thirteen was found in a house in Los Angeles. She had been kept in a back room since she was a baby, tied to a chair by day and shut in a crib at night, and nobody had spoken to her. The doctors called her Genie to protect her name.
