She learned words quickly once she was out — hundreds of them. She never learned to put them in order. She could say want milk; she could never say I would like some milk, please, and no amount of teaching got her there. The scientists who worked with her concluded that there is a window in a child’s early years when the brain is built to take in grammar, and that if nothing comes in through the window, it shuts.

A hundred and fifty years before, in 1828, a boy of about sixteen walked into the city of Nuremberg in Germany holding a letter. He could say a few sentences and write one name — Kaspar Hauser. He said he had been kept in a dark cell all his life, fed bread and water, and had never seen a human face. He learned to speak afterwards, and to write, and he spoke strangely for the rest of his short life, like a man translating from a language only he knew.

The boy in this book went into the cellar at six. He had six years of sunlight and talk in him already; the window was open and things had come through. And he was spoken to every day — one voice, a cook’s, and the radio through the wall, and a brother on Thursdays, and books. So his language did not close. It grew, but it grew crooked, fed on one woman’s kitchen Persian and one novel from another century, read two hundred times. That is why he sounds the way he sounds. He is not slow. He is a man who learned to talk from one old novel and a radio through a wall. Which novel, he has not said.

Faces need practice. In the 1990s, after the fall of the dictatorship in Romania, the world found out about the state orphanages. Tens of thousands of children had been kept in rows of cots, fed and changed on a schedule, and otherwise left. They were not beaten. They were not spoken to, or held, or looked at. A team of American scientists began following some of them in the year 2000 and has followed them ever since, and what they found was this: a child who is not looked at does not learn to look. Those children grew up unable to read a face — to tell a frown from a smile, or to care which was which. Some could not attach to anyone. Some attached to everyone, instantly, with no difference between a mother and a stranger in a shop.

The boy in this book has seen one face in twenty-two years, and that one by candle. He cannot read yours. He reads the thing he has had instead: sound. Breath, footstep, the weight on a stair, the pitch of a voice through iron. He knows you are lying by how you set down a plate.

The body remembers the open and fears it. People who have spent years in a cell alone — in the isolation units of American prisons, which a doctor named Stuart Grassian began studying in the 1980s, and which have since been studied by many others — come out and find that the world attacks them. Light hurts. Noise hurts. A room with more than two people in it is unbearable. An open sky makes the legs go. Men held as hostages in Lebanon in the 1980s, some of them for more than six years, chained in small rooms, wrote afterwards about their first hour outside: not joy — panic, in the body, that the mind could not talk down.
That is why the sky in this book is written the way it is.

And here is the thing the book turns on. Most people in long isolation come apart. The studies agree. They stop sleeping at proper hours, stop washing, talk to themselves, see things, rage, go flat. The walls come inside.

But a few do the opposite. A few build. A navy commander held alone in Hanoi for years kept himself whole with routine and memory and a code of rules he set for himself and would not break. A man in the state of Maine walked into the woods in 1986 and lived alone there for twenty-seven years, stealing food from cabins, speaking to no one — not one word, by his own count, in all that time except a single hi to a hiker — and when he was caught in 2013 he was lucid, strange, and in some ways clearer than the people who questioned him. And in a cellar in Austria, a woman kept underground by her father for twenty-four years raised three children who never saw daylight until 2008, and she had taught them to read and write down there, by lamplight, with nothing but what was handed down the stairs.

What those people had in common, as far as anyone can tell, was three things. Something to read or remember. One voice, however rarely. And a rule — something they had decided about themselves, early, and held to.

The boy in this book had four hundred books, a cook, a brother on Thursdays, and a rule. The rule was the cook’s: you are kept, so behave like something worth keeping. He built a life on that sentence. It is not the life you or I would have built. But it stood for twenty-two years, which is longer than most houses.

One more thing, about what the room was full of. Every Thursday night for twenty-two years a fistful of esfand was burned on coals at the head of those stairs, for the eye, and the smoke went down, as smoke in a stairwell does, into a closed room with one small vent. Esfand is wild rue — Peganum harmala [PEG-ah-num har-MAH-lah] in the books — and its seeds hold two substances, harmine [HAR-meen] and harmaline [HAR-mah-leen], that are the same ones in the vine the peoples of the Amazon brew into ayahuasca [eye-ah-WAH-skah] to see the dead. A pinch on the coals is a blessing. A room full of it, night after night for twenty years, with the seeds in the evening tea besides, is something else: a slow, dreaming wakefulness, voices that answer, pictures behind the eyes, and a clarity that feels like truth. Persian doctors wrote about it a thousand years ago. It is in every kitchen in the country and nobody asks. The boy in this book breathed it for twenty-two years.
He calls the thing he built the second door. The scientists would have another name for it. He would not care what it was. He would ask you whether it worked, and you would have to say that it did.
III. THURSDAYS
I kept the exercise book inside the cookbook and the cookbook on the kitchen table and I worked at it in the mornings with the radio on, and Touran cut onions, and nobody asked.

Every Thursday was the same now. The tea at a quarter to eleven, with the seeds in the bottom. The laundry floor. Touran going past the door with the brass dish and the smoke coming back along the concrete to find me. I was not frightened of it any more. I waited for it the way you wait for a friend.

The Thursdays came out in pieces. Not sentences — pieces. Words with gaps around them where I had missed a run or got a long for a short. Like hearing two people through a wall when the television is on.

TAP CODE — III
Lamps, mirrors, pipes
A short note before the last part. This one is about how people have said the thing that mattered when they could not open the door.
Long before the telegraph, people sent words with light.

The Greeks used fire on hilltops; a chain of them could carry the news of a city’s fall across a sea in a night. The Romans used polished shields. In the 1800s the British army built a machine called a heliograph — a mirror on a tripod that caught the sun and flashed it, long and short, in Morse, to another mirror on another hill fifty kilometres away. It was used in the deserts of India and Africa and in the American West, and it worked only when the sun was out, and it carried orders and warnings and, now and then, a message from a man who thought he would not see the other hill again.

At sea the navies used a lamp with shutters. A sailor stood on the bridge and worked a lever, and the shutters opened and closed, and across a mile of black water another sailor read the flashes and wrote them down. Ships talked to each other that way through two world wars, because a lamp cannot be overheard the way a radio can. The last message a ship sent before it went down was sometimes a lamp, long and short, to a ship that could not reach it in time.

In prisons, where there is no sun and no sea, the tool was anything. A tin cup on a bar. A shoe on a pipe. In the camps of the Soviet Union prisoners held small mirrors through the bars and tilted them to catch a face in the next block. In cells with a shared water line men learned that the iron carried a knock three floors, clearer than a shout.

And lovers, of course. A lamp in a window. A particular curtain drawn or not drawn. A song played at a certain hour. People who could not be seen together have always found a way to say still here, and the way has always been the same: something small, repeated, at a time agreed, that means nothing to anyone who does not know, and everything to the one who does.
Here is what all of those have in common, and it is the only thing this note is really for.
The message that matters is never the long one.

The long messages — the orders, the news, the arguments, the hour of talk on a Thursday — are what the code is for. But the one that keeps a person alive is the short one at the end. Sleep tight through a wall in Hanoi. A single flash from a hill at sundown. A cup on a bar, twice, at lights out. It does not carry information. Both sides already know everything it says. It carries only this: I am still on the other side of this. I have not gone. Go to sleep.
In the house in this book it is four knocks and two. It is the shortest thing in the code and it has been sent more than seven thousand times. It was sent tonight. It will be sent tomorrow.
Nobody above the floor has ever asked what it means. The child says it back in her head. That is correct. That is all it has ever wanted.
IV. SKY

In Iran the dead have a night of the week. Thursday night, the night before Friday, is theirs: you visit the grave, you light a candle, you give out food in their name to whoever is passing, and the giving is called khairat [khey-RAHT] — charity for a soul. Every Thursday night the city does this a little. On the last Thursday of the year, the one before Nowruz, the whole city does it at once. The roads to Behesht-e Zahra are solid from noon. The graves are washed. Families sit on the stones with the photographs and the halva and the oranges and the children running, and anyone still at home that night is at home because they have nobody in the ground, or because they cannot bear to go.

In that house nobody went. The old man had not been to the cemetery since 2004. The graves were tended by a man he paid. Instead the cloth was laid in the upstairs hall, the way the khanom had laid it when she was alive, and the house kept its dead at home.

Touran laid it. She had laid it every year for twenty-two years and knew where everything went without thinking: the table in the hall under the silver photograph, the white cloth, a mirror, the Quran open on its stand, a bowl of water with a sprig of green in it, candles. Dates. A plate of oranges — the oranges he was always being told to eat. Rosewater in a small bottle for the hands. And the halva, the dark one, which she had stood over for an hour that afternoon with the radio off, stirring, and spread on three plates and marked with the back of a spoon.

Three photographs along the back of the cloth. The little one, laughing, his eyes shut — the one from the silver frame. Zal at six, in a school smock, serious, looking straight at the camera with a face that was the face in the cellar with twenty-two years taken off it. And a woman I had not seen before, older than the one in Yasmin’s room, in a dress from the eighties, with Babak’s bones in her face and Zal’s stillness. The khanom. The mother. Touran set her photograph between the two boys and straightened it twice.

There was no photograph of Yasmin’s mother. Babak had not brought one down, and nobody asked him to, and Yasmin did not seem to notice, and I did not say anything, because I knew now what I would have been saying.

The old man sat in a chair at the end of the hall and watched, with his hands on his knees, and said nothing, and did not leave. Yasmin helped. I helped. When it was laid Touran sent me down to the gate with a tray of the halva and a stack of paper plates, to give to whoever passed, in the name of the dead of the house, and I stood in Fereshteh Street in the cold for an hour handing halva to drivers and maids and a boy on a motorbike, who all said God accept it and did not ask whose it was, and none of them looked at the house.
When I came up the plate in front of the boy in the school smock had a piece gone from it, and Touran’s apron pocket was full, the way it had been every year.
That was the afternoon. The night was the night.

I was there. I want that understood. I did not watch from the stairs; I went down with them. I do not know why they let me, except that by then I was one of them and there was nobody left to hide it from.

Touran went first, at midnight, with the plate, and with the halva in her apron. One step, both feet. Then Babak, behind her, in the clothes he wore around the house, no jacket, no shoes, carrying nothing. Then me. The door beside the refrigerator was open all the way for the first time in my life in that house. The corridor. The laundry. Touran’s room. The stair.

He was standing. He had never been standing when I came down; he was always at the table or on the bed. He was standing in the middle of the swept floor with the candle behind him, and he had on the clothes he always wore — Babak’s old things, I had understood long ago, handed down through Touran — and he had washed, and somebody had cut his hair, badly, with love.
Babak stopped on the bottom step.

I do not know what I had expected. I had read twenty years of them. I had thought, I suppose, that there would be something — that they would say something, or one of them would go to the other. They did not. They had said it all. Every Thursday for twenty years they had said it all, and there was nothing left over, and they stood there, one on the step and one on the floor, two men with the same bones and the same stillness, and looked.

Babak looked at his brother’s face. Zal looked at his brother’s hands, and his feet, and the rise of his breathing. And then — I saw it — he lifted his eyes, with effort, the way you lift something heavy, and looked at Babak’s face. He held it. He was not reading it; he could not read faces. He was memorising it. It was the third face he had ever had, after Touran’s and mine, and he was putting it away behind the door with the sky.
“You have Baba’s forehead,” he said at last, in the voice from the old radio. “I did not know that. Touran never said.”
Babak made a sound that was not a word.

The study key was on the table, beside the book, squared to the edge: an old brass key on a loop of string. Babak had put it there when he came in, without my seeing him do it; it was the first thing of his that had ever been in that room. Now he came down off the step and picked it up again, and in the same movement, without being asked, took the plate from Touran’s hands. Rice, stew, chicken, the round of bread folded over. He stood holding it like a man who has been handed his own child.
“Eat it while it’s hot,” Touran said. Her voice was perfectly steady. “And the orange.”

Zal went past his brother to the stairs. He stopped at the bottom and put his hand on the wall, where I had put mine the first night, where Touran put hers every night, where the stone was worn smooth and dark from twenty-two years of one hand going up and down. He stood with his palm against it for a moment.
“The fourth step is damp,” he said, to nobody. And then, to his brother, without turning round, in the voice of the book: “Sabr kon va omidvar bash.” And went up.

Touran went after him, slowly. I was last. At the top I turned and looked back down into the yellow room, and Babak was sitting at the table with the plate in front of him, and he had lifted the cover, and the smell came up, and he turned his head toward it the way a plant turns toward a window. Then he got up, and crossed the room, and shot the bolt on the cellar’s own door — I heard it go, iron on iron, from the top of the stair — and that was the first time in twenty-two years anyone had.

He did not go out that night. Touran would not let him. “Not in the dark,” she said. “You’ll see it first with the light on it, like a decent person.” So he sat in the kitchen all night in Touran’s chair with a blanket round him, with the back door shut and the curtain drawn, and Touran sat with him, and I sat with them, and nobody slept. He did not say much. Once he said, “It is very loud up here,” though the house was silent, and I understood that he meant the size of it — the ceilings, the space the sound had to go into. Once he asked what the refrigerator was and we told him and he went and stood in front of it with the door open for a long time, looking at the sholeh zard.
At six Touran drew the curtain.
I am going to tell this slowly because it was slow. It was the slowest thing I have ever watched a person do.

The garden was grey. It was March, a few days before the new year; there was mist on the grass and the arghavan was bare and black, a month from flowering, against a sky that was going from grey to white. Touran opened the back door. The cold came in and the smell of wet earth. He stood up out of the chair and the blanket fell off him and he walked to the door and stopped on the sill, with the kitchen behind him and the garden in front, and he looked up.

His legs went first. Not a fall — a folding, as if the strings had been let out. He went down onto his knees on the sill with his hands on the frame of the door either side, holding on, and his head went back, and he stayed like that, looking straight up, with his mouth open. His eyes were streaming. Not crying; I do not think he knew how; just water, running, the way your eyes run when you walk out of a cinema at noon. He was breathing in short pulls, high in his chest, as if the air were too big to get down.

Touran did not go to him. She stood by the stove with her arms folded and her face shut. I understood that she had decided this on the stairs twenty-two years ago, that this was his and not hers, and that she would not take it from him by helping.
I went to the door. I could not not. I stood on the sill where he was, close enough to feel the shaking, the whole body going the way a dog shakes.
“It is bigger than you said,” he said, up at the sky, not to me. His voice was almost steady. “You said big. You should have said this.”
“I didn’t have the word.”
“No.” He breathed. “There is not one.”

He stayed on his knees for a long time. The sky went from white to the thin blue it is in Tehran in March, when the smog lifts for a week before Nowruz, and a plane went over very high, and he followed it with his eyes all the way across until it was gone and then went on looking at the place where it had been. And then — I felt it stop — the shaking stopped. Not slowly. All at once, the way the knocking stopped at the end of a Thursday. He had done something inside. He had looked at what was happening to his body, at the legs and the breath and the eyes, with his whole attention, the way he looked at a plate — and he had filed it.
“That is what it does,” he said. “All right.”

He got up. He did it the way an old man does, one hand on the door frame, but he did it, and stood on the sill and then stepped down onto the wet grass in socks, and stood on it, and looked down at the feet in it, and then walked.

Not far. To the middle of the lawn. He walked the way you walk on ice — too carefully, with his arms a little out — and he stopped under the arghavan and put his hand on the trunk and looked up into the bare branches for a long moment.
“It is not purple,” he said.
“It’s March. There aren’t any flowers yet.”
“I know. I am saying it anyway. For the record.”
And then the bird.

It was on the grass by the wall. A dove, a grey one, the fat kind that are everywhere in the city, pecking at nothing. He saw it — I saw him see it, the whole of him turning toward it the way he turned toward the plate — and he went very still, and then he was not still, and it was over. I did not see him move. One moment he was under the tree and the next he was by the wall with the thing in his hands and its neck already gone, and he had bitten into it — into the breast of it, through the feathers — before I had taken a breath to shout.
He stood there and chewed. The feathers were on his mouth. He looked at it in his hands with interest, turned it over, bit again.
“It is better than the pigeon,” he said, with his mouth full. “The pigeon had been in the shaft for a day.”
Touran, behind me in the kitchen door, made a sound I had never heard her make and have never heard since.

He finished what he wanted of it. It did not take long; he had had practice. He put the rest down on the grass, neatly, the way he put down a plate, and wiped his mouth with the back of his hand and looked at the blood on his hand with the same interest and wiped it on the grass.
Then he walked to the gate.

The gardener who came on Tuesdays had left it unlatched on the Tuesday; Touran had seen to that, I think, though she never said. He put his hand on it and it opened. Beyond it was the street — the pavement, the wall of the house opposite, a parked car, a woman in a chador [chah-DOR] carrying bread. Nobody looked. Nobody ever looks.
He stepped through. He did not look back.

I thought he would. I had read it in a hundred books — the last look, the hand raised. He did not know that was a thing people did. Nobody had ever left him; nobody had ever had the chance. He stepped through the gate in his socks with feathers on his shirt and walked away down the street toward the park, too carefully, with his arms a little out, and the gate swung to behind him, and he was gone.

I stood on the wet grass and understood, finally, with the thing on the lawn by the wall and Touran’s sound still in my ears, that I had not let a prisoner out. I had let something out. It had been in that house for twenty-two years and it had never once been a prisoner, and now it was in the street.
When I went in there were feathers on the sill. I swept them. Touran was at the stove with her back to me and did not turn round, and she did not turn round for the rest of that day.
The house did what the house does. It agreed not to notice.

The old man was told nothing. He saw his son at breakfast and at dinner, in the dim dining room with the curtains half drawn, across a table for twelve, and his son said Baba and the old man said pesaram [peh-sah-RAM] — my son — and that was all they had ever said, and nothing had changed. I served, and cleared, and did not look at the chair, because I had learned the house’s first rule by then and could keep it with the best of them. In the afternoons the old man slept. He had agreed not to notice things for twenty-two years, and a son is a son in a dark room when you have decided not to look at him; they had the same bones.

The office was told that Babak had gone to the Nowshahr house. Babak sent the email himself, from the study, the night before he went down; he had thought of everything, or his brother had. The company was the old man’s and ran itself and nobody from it ever came to the house.
Touran made five plates. She set one on the end of the counter at nine. At a quarter past midnight she took it down, one step, both feet.
And at eleven the pipe knocked. Four. A pause. Two.
Yasmin, in her bed, with her eyes shut: “That’s the house saying goodnight.” And said it back in her head. And slept.

It was Babak knocking now. From below. And nothing answered from above, because the study was empty, and the man who had answered for twenty years was somewhere in a city of fifteen million with no name and no papers and feathers on his shirt. I lay in the big bed on the closed floor and listened to the four and the two go up through the house and find nothing, and I did not knock back on the bedframe. I could not. I did not know who I would be saying it to.

I went down once. A week after. I do not know why — to see, I suppose. The plate I had left outside the door the night before was on the bottom step, finished, the fork laid parallel to the knife. The bolt was shot on the inside. I stood at the bottom of the stair and said his name through the door, and after a while his voice came back, Babak’s voice, which I had only ever heard say good morning and she has swimming on Thursdays, and it had already started to change — slower, with the edges off, the voice of a man who has stopped talking to anyone who can see him.
“Nasrin.”
“Yes.”
A pause. Then: “Sakht bood? [SAKHT bood] Was it difficult?”
I stood there in the cold. I did not know which thing he meant. The sky. The bird. The gate. The number. Her.
“Yes,” I said, which was true of all of them, and went up.
Touran died in July, in the heat.

She died in her room beside the laundry, in her bed, in the night, with the radio off and her shoes side by side under the chair and a clean plate ready on the chair for the morning. The doctor who came said her heart, and wrote it down, and nobody asked him anything, because that was not a house where you asked.

I found her. I had come down at six because her door was not open and it was always open by six, and I knew before I knocked, the way she had always known things. I sat with her for a while before I went up to tell the old man. I held the hand with the crooked finger. She had told me a drawer and I had let it be a drawer, and I thought about that, sitting there — about how much of loving somebody in that house was letting things be what they said they were.

Touran had heart pills. A brown bottle in the kitchen drawer by the radio, one in the morning and one at night; she had had them since before I came. She never counted them. Touran never counted anything; that was my job. When I cleared her room I found the bottle in her apron pocket, and it was empty, and I stood there and did the arithmetic I had never done while she was alive, and it did not come out.
I went down that night with the plate and stood at the bottom of the stair and said through the door: “Her pills.”

A long silence. Then Babak’s voice, with the edges off. “He told me in March. The last Thursday, after you’d stopped writing. He said Touran was the only one in the house who had ever been inside that room, and that she would never let me stay down there, not for a night. He said she would not last the summer if nobody counted the bottle, and that nobody counted the bottle.” A breath. “I counted it. In June. I come up at four, when the house is asleep; I always have. There were nine left and she thought there were thirty. I did not tell her. I did not tell you. I put the plate on the chair for her every night so she would not have to come down, and she came down anyway, and I did not say anything.”
“He didn’t touch her.”
“He has never touched anyone. He arranges.” The bolt did not move. “Was it difficult, you asked me once. That was.”
I stood there with the plate going cold in my hands. Then I asked the thing I had never asked, in a year and a half, because I had been taught not to.
“The book. The one on the table. What was it?”
Another silence, longer. When he spoke it was almost gently, the way you tell a child something it should have been told years ago.

“You never looked? No. He wouldn’t have let you. Go and buy a copy, Nasrin. Any bookstall has it. Read it to the end. Then come back down and tell me whether he improved on it. I’ve had twenty years and I still can’t decide.”
And he told me the name.
The plate stayed on the chair. I took it down at nine that night. I have taken it down every night since.

The old man’s lawyer came in September and said the house would be sold. He said it to the old man in the dining room and the old man said nothing and did not disagree, the way he did not disagree with anything now. He would go to the Nowshahr house, the lawyer said, where the air was better. There was a nurse there. Arrangements had been made. The lawyer did not say by whom. I knew by whom; there was only one person in that house who made arrangements, and he was under the floor, and he had thought of everything.

The staff came with the sale. That was in the papers, the lawyer told the buyers — a long-serving household, very discreet, the nanny particularly; the child was leaving with the grandfather but the nanny could stay on if the new owners had children, which they did. A reference, the lawyer said. A very good reference.

Yasmin left in October, in the dark blue car, with the old man and the nurse and a driver, for Nowshahr. She held my hand on the steps the way she had held it the first day, like the rail of a bus. She had been told her father had gone ahead to open the house. She had not been told anything else. She was seven.
“Will the house still say goodnight,” she said, “in Nowshahr?”
“I don’t know, dokhtaram.”
“I’ll say it anyway. In my head.” She considered. “You say it back. From here. Then it’s the same.”
“All right.”

She got in the car. It went out through the gate the gardener had left unlatched seven months before and I never saw her again, and every night at eleven I say it, from here, in my head, so that it is the same.
I bought it on the Friday.

There is a man at the bottom of the hill, by the park, who sells used books off a blanket — the same man every week, the same blanket, paperbacks gone soft as bread. I had walked past him seventy Fridays. That Friday I stopped and said the name Babak had given me, and he had it, because everybody has it: Kont-e Mont Kristo [KONT-eh mont KREES-toh] — The Count of Monte Cristo — a fat cheap paperback with a ship on the cover, eleven hundred pages, for the price of two kilos of rice. He said it was a good one. He said his father had read it in prison, in the Shah’s time, and then again in the other one’s.
I read it in my room on the closed floor, at night, after the four and two that nobody answered. It took me nine days. I am not a fast reader and the words are long.
I am not going to tell you the story of that book here; it is told next, plainly, for anyone who has not read it. I will tell you only what it did to me, in order.

For the first hundred pages I thought: this is a sailor in France two hundred years ago, what has it to do with anything. A young man, about to be married, about to be made captain, and three men who hate him for it, and a letter.

Then he was arrested, and nobody told him why, and he was taken in a boat at night to a prison on a rock, and put under the ground. And I put the book down on the bed and looked at the wall for a while.

Then — on perhaps the fourth night — the prisoner heard a scratching inside the stone of his cell, and it was another man, and they began to talk through the wall. And I understood that I was not reading a book. I was reading the pipe.

I read faster after that. I read the way you read when you are frightened of what is on the next page and cannot stop. The priest in the next cell teaching the sailor everything he knew, year after year, through a hole in the stone, until the ignorant boy was the most educated man in France and had never seen the sun. The priest working out, from nothing but what the boy told him, exactly who had put him there, and why — and the boy going white, because he had never known. The priest dying. The sack.

I will not tell you the sack. I will only say that when I read that chapter — the old man’s weak heart, the third attack, the little bottle, the boy counting out the drops and the drops not being enough — I got up and went down the back stairs in my socks at three in the morning and stood outside the cellar door with my hand on the wood, and did not knock, and went back up, and sat on the bed until it was light, with the empty bottle from Touran’s apron on the blanket beside the book.

And then the second half. The man coming back from the sea with a new name and more money than God, and taking years — years — to arrange the ruin of the three men and the prosecutor, so patiently, so carefully, from so far behind the curtain, that each of them did the thing that destroyed him with his own hands and thanked the Count for the advice. A servant placed in this house. A marriage arranged in that one. A word in the right ear at the right dinner. Never once his own hand raised. I am only an instrument, he says, when a woman begs him to stop. And a girl, rescued, raised in the dark of his plans, who becomes the one thing he loves.
I finished it at four in the morning on the ninth day. The last words of the book are two. Wait and hope.

I took the exercise book out of the drawer and laid it open on the bed beside the novel, and I began to go through the Thursdays again from the beginning, with the book open next to them. Not reading them this time. Matching them.

The wall, and the voice through it. The old keeper who could not be told. The maid sent away with a good letter — a servant placed, a servant removed. The wife chosen because she would look the other way, and the chapter where she looked. I am only an instrument. The girl raised in the dark of the plans. There is neither happiness nor misery in the world. The swap. The improvement. And me — the agency, the four girls, does she count things — the servant put into the enemy’s house, except that the house was the enemy and the servant was me.
It took me a week to be sure. I was sure.

He had read it two hundred and eleven times. He had told me himself, the first week, before I knew what he was telling me: it is the only account of people and what they do that I have ever had. I had thought he meant it the way you mean my favourite book. He had meant it the way you mean the instructions. Every Thursday for twenty years had been a chapter. The house had been the book. I had been living in it, and so had everyone I loved in that place, and none of us had read it.

I went down and told Babak through the door that I had finished it. He asked what I thought. I said I did not know whether it was better. He said that was the right answer, and that he had the plate, and that I could go up.
TAP CODE — IV
The man in the sack

One more note, late, because it could not come earlier. Nasrin has read the book now and has told you only what it did to her. Somebody has to tell you what is in it, for anyone who has not read it, because the house has been living inside it for twenty-two years and so have you, since the first page. Here it is, plainly. It is long; so is the book.

The Count of Monte Cristo was written by Alexandre Dumas and came out in Paris in 1844, in pieces, in a newspaper, the way long books did then. It is about eleven hundred pages. It has been in print ever since and translated into every language that has a printing press. The copy on the table in the cellar is the old Persian one — the translation made by a Qajar [ghah-JAR] prince, Taher Mirza [TAH-her meer-ZAH], in the reign of Naser al-Din Shah [NAH-ser od-DEEN shah], more than a hundred and twenty years ago, and reprinted ever since in the same long sentences. Its words are older than anyone alive, which is why the man who learned to talk from it sounds the way he does.

The first part. The boy. Marseille, 1815. Edmond Dantès [ed-MON dan-TESS] is nineteen, a sailor, about to be made captain of his ship and about to marry a girl called Mercédès [mer-say-DESS]. Three men want what he has: one wants his job, one wants his girl, one is simply jealous. Between them they write a letter to the police saying he is carrying a message for Napoleon, who is in exile and whom the government fears. It is not true, but there is a scrap of paper in his pocket that makes it look true. He is arrested at his own engagement dinner.

The prosecutor who questions him sees at once that the boy is innocent. But the paper in his pocket is addressed to the prosecutor’s own father, and if that comes out the prosecutor is finished. So he burns the paper in front of the boy, tells him he is free, and has him taken that night, in a boat, to the Château d’If [shah-TOH DEEF] — a fortress on a rock in the sea — and put in a cell under the ground. Nobody tells him why. His father starves. His girl waits, and then marries the man who wanted her. The world is told he is gone.

The second part. The wall. He is there fourteen years. For the first years he goes nearly mad; he stops eating, he prays, he rages, he decides to die. Then one night he hears scratching inside the stone. It is another prisoner, an old priest called Faria [fah-REE-ah], who has spent years digging a tunnel in the wrong direction and has come out in the boy’s cell by mistake.

They talk through the wall, and then through the hole, every night for years. The old man has nothing but his memory, and his memory is everything a man could know — languages, history, science, how people think and why they lie. He teaches all of it to the boy. He makes him, in the dark, the most educated man in France. And one night he asks the boy to tell him his whole story, every detail — who was at the dinner, who stood where, who said what — and from nothing but that, sitting in the dark, he works out exactly who framed the boy and why. The boy has never once suspected. He goes white. He sits with it. He has no door to go through.

The old priest has a weak heart. He has had two attacks and knows the third will kill him. He keeps a small bottle of red drops that can bring him back from the edge, and he tells the boy how many to give, and when. The third attack comes. The boy gives the drops. They are not enough.

The third part. The sack. The guards sew the old man’s body into a sack to throw into the sea, which is what that prison does with its dead. They leave it in the cell overnight. The boy carries the body through the tunnel into his own cell and lays it in his own bed, and cuts the sack open, and gets inside, and sews it shut from within with the priest’s needle. In the morning the guards carry him out thinking he is the dead man, swing him three times, and throw him off the rock. He has a knife. He cuts his way out underwater. He comes up out of the sea with no name, no papers, and nobody alive who knows his face.
Somebody had to die for the prisoner to leave. That is the chapter. That is the only way out of the book’s prison, and the man in the cellar has read it two hundred and eleven times.

The fourth part. The arrangement. The priest had told him where a fortune was buried. He finds it. He takes a new name, the Count of Monte Cristo, and he spends ten years becoming somebody nobody could recognise — and then he goes to Paris, where the three men and the prosecutor have all become rich and respectable, and he ruins them.

He never raises his hand. That is what the second half of the book is about. He puts a servant into one man’s house. He arranges a marriage in another. He drops a word at a dinner and a banker’s credit collapses. He finds the one secret each man has buried and arranges for it to come up on its own, in public, at the worst moment. Each of them does the thing that destroys him with his own hands, and several of them thank the Count for his advice while they do it. One kills himself. One goes mad on the floor of his own garden. One is left alive and poor, on purpose, because the Count has decided that is worse. When a woman begs him to stop, he tells her he is only an instrument, and that what is happening is justice, and that justice is not his.

Along the way he buys a girl out of slavery, Haydée [hy-DAY], the daughter of a murdered prince, and raises her in his house, in the dark of his plans, and she is the only person in the book he comes to love.

The last page. When it is done, he sails away with her. He leaves a letter for the only young couple he has not harmed. It ends with the sentence the man in the cellar says most, and the one the whole book was written to arrive at: All human wisdom is contained in these two words — wait and hope.

That is the book. Read it beside the house and you will see what Nasrin saw. A boy put under the ground for something a brother did. A voice through a wall. An old keeper with a weak heart and a bottle nobody counts. A man who never raises his hand. A girl raised in the dark. And a prisoner who has read the only way out so many times that he has decided to improve on it.
He says he has. There is one chapter left, and it is a year later, and nothing in it is in the book.
V. THE THIRTEENTH DAY
That was a year ago. I am still here.

The new people made their money in Dubai and brought it home. He does something with steel; she does something with charities. They have a girl of five and a boy who is still a baby, and the girl is a nice child, quiet, and she likes to be read to, and I do not skip the long words. They have painted the hall and taken down the silver photograph and put up something modern. They have not been into the back. Nobody goes into the back. There is a cook who comes in by the day and goes home at eight, and after she has gone I make one more plate, and cover it, and set it on the end of the counter, and at a quarter past midnight I take it down. The envelope comes on the first of every month from a bank in Nowshahr. I do not know whose name is on the account and I have never asked. I have learned not to ask. It took me a while but I have learned.

Today was the last Thursday of the year. The new people laid a cloth — the khanom’s mother insisted; she wanted the children to have the traditions — and it is a pretty thing, in the hall under the modern picture, with the mirror and the candles and the Quran on its stand. There are no photographs on it. They have no dead here yet. The khanom ordered the halva from a confectioner in Zafaraniyeh and it is very good, better than Touran’s, and I have taken a piece off the plate and put it in the pocket of my apron, because it would be a waste otherwise.
At eleven the pipe knocked. Four. A pause. Two.
I was in the back corridor. I had my hand on the iron where the old pipe runs along the party wall, and I felt it come up through the metal.

And then — I felt this too; I have felt it every night for five months and it has not stopped being the strangest thing in my life — the answer came. Not from above. The study is the Agha’s office now and he was asleep. From the side. From the wall of the back corridor that the house shares with the house next door, the party wall, where the old pipes run between the two servants’ quarters because the houses were built together in the fifties by brothers who did not get on.
Four. A pause. Two.
Ha.

The house next door hired a new gardener in the autumn. I have seen him over the wall, from the window of the closed floor, which is my floor. He is thin and pale and he does not speak to the other staff; the maid there told me at the park that he is simple, a little, from somewhere in the north, with no family, a good worker, very quiet, very tidy, keeps his room like a soldier. He wears a hat always. He stands under their arghavan sometimes for a long time looking up into it, even when there is nothing to see.
He has a row of small skulls on his windowsill. The maid told me that too, at the park, with a face. Mice and birds and one bigger one. By size.

I have never gone to the wall. I have never knocked on it, or called over it, or gone round to the gate of the house next door, which is thirty steps from ours, and asked. He knows I am here. He hears everything; he has always heard everything. If he wanted me he would knock. He knocks to one person, at eleven, and that person knocks back, and it is not me, and that is correct.

I have stopped decoding. The exercise book is in the drawer in my room with the cartoon dog on the cover and I have not opened it since last March. I do not need to. I know what they say to each other. They say yes.

The paperback with the ship on the cover is in the drawer beside it. I have read it twice more since the summer, looking for the chapter that comes after the one we are in. There is not one. The book ends on a boat going out to sea, with the man and the girl he raised, and two words, and nothing about the house they left behind or the ones still in it. I know what he is waiting for. I have never worked out what he hopes.

I took the plate down tonight. One step, both feet, a hand on the wall where the stone is dark. I set it on the floor outside the door, with the bread beside it on a saucer, and I knocked three times, softly, the way he used to for Touran, so that the man inside would know it was me and could take his time.
After a while the bolt went back and the door opened a hand’s width and the plate went in, and the saucer, and the door shut, and the bolt went home.

I had turned to go up. I had my hand on the wall. And his voice came through the wood behind me, slow, with the edges off, the voice of a man who has been talking to a pipe for a year — and it was his brother’s voice now, exactly; I would not have known them apart.
“Nasrin. The cloth. Did they use a good photograph?”
I stood on the stair with my hand on the stone.
“Yes,” I said. “A very good one.”
It was the first lie I had told in that house. I understood, on the stair, that it would not be the last, and that this was how it was done — one plate, one photograph, one yes at a time.
And went up.

He opened the door on the thirteenth day of the new year — Sizdah Bedar [seez-DAH beh-DAR], the day the whole city goes out to the parks and the hills to throw the bad luck of the year into running water, and the house was empty but for the two of us and the old pipes. I had not asked. I had stopped asking things in that house a long time ago; it was the one thing it had taught me that stayed learned.
I had set the plate down outside as always and knocked three times, softly, and turned to go up, and the bolt went back behind me, and the door opened — not a hand’s width. All the way.
“Come in, Nasrin,” Babak said. “You’ve never seen it with the light on.”

He had a candle. He had the same candle, in the same saucer, in the centre of the same table. He was sitting on the bed, which was made with military tightness, because Touran had made it that way every morning for twenty-two years and he had learned how from watching her through the door the one time he came down at sixteen, and he was thin, and pale the way nothing above ground is pale, and his hair had been cut by somebody who could not see very well, which was him. He had the book open on his knee. He looked at my feet, and my hands, and the rise of my breathing, and then — with effort, the way you lift something — at my face.
“Look at the room,” he said. “Properly. You never did. You looked at him.”
I looked.

The shelves. The bed. The bucket in the corner with its lid on, dry; it had always been dry; Touran had never once had to empty it and I had never once asked why. The vent, grey. The shelf under it with the small skulls in a row by size — rats, which Touran had killed in her kitchen for thirty years and could not bring herself to throw in the bin, because the little one had liked small bones; a pigeon that had come down the shaft dead in 2011; a cat with a collar, which had got in under the door in 2017, in the fortnight Touran was in hospital with her knees and nobody came down, and was dead when she came back, and whose collar was in the drawer because Touran could not throw that away either. The book on the table. The Scout manual lying flat on top of the shelf where a hand could find it in the dark. And the bolt on the inside of the door, iron, old, which the old man had fitted in the first winter so that the boy could lock himself in and feel safer, and which had never once been shot until Babak shot it in March, because for twenty-two years there had been nobody on this side of it to shoot it.

“He died the first winter,” Babak said. “January, 2005, in the week of the longest cold. He was six and the cellar is cold and Baba would not have a stove down here in case the house smelled of it. Touran found him. Baba put him under the arghavan himself, at night; the stone at Behesht-e Zahra was already paid for and already had his name on it. There’s a stone in the Behesht-e Zahra with his name on it and there’s nothing under it. Touran has set a plate every night since. In this country you feed the dead; you know that; you’ve seen her apron on the last Thursday of the year. She never lied to you. Go back over everything she said to you and you will find she never once told you he was alive. He has always been a good boy.”
I did not sit down. There was only the one chair and it was not correct.

“I was eleven,” he said. “Two years after. I had the manual and I had the pipe and I had a brother under the floor who I had put there, and one night I knocked, and I knocked back. I have done it every Thursday for twenty years. Both hands in those books are mine. You put your hand on the pipe and felt it all come down from above and you told yourself half of it came from below, because you needed it to. So did I. For twenty years I have had somebody to tell me the thing I could not say and then do it, and it was never me, it was him. The maid. Her. Touran’s bottle.” He looked at the book on his knee. “He talks like this because I do. I had read it two hundred times by the time I was twenty. I threw it down the stairs because I could not stand to have it in the study any more, and then I had him read it to me through the pipe instead.”
“And me.”

“And you.” He was quiet for a while. “There is one more thing you should have, and then I’ve nothing left. Touran burned a fistful of esfand at the top of these stairs every Thursday night for twenty-two years, for the eye, and the smoke goes down, and there is one vent. She put the seeds in your tea on the nights you came down; she put them in mine, at sixteen, the one time I came. Do you know what the seed is? The same thing that is in the vine the Indians drink in the jungle to see their dead. It is in every kitchen in this country and nobody asks. I came down at sixteen and sat in the smoke for one hour, and he was here, on that bed, and he told me not to come again, and I didn’t. You sat in it for a year. With the setar coming down the pipe on top of it — hers; Baba forbade music in the house after the roof and I have played it in that study every Thursday since I was eleven with the door locked, quietly, before I knock, because it was the only thing of hers I had.” He looked at me. “I am not saying the smoke made him. The smoke doesn’t make anything. It only lets what is already in you stand up and talk. Baba made him first, on the stones, with his hand on the little one’s chest. Touran made him with the plate. I made him with the pipe. The whole street made him by never asking. And you came down the stairs with the plate and he was here waiting for you, because he is always here waiting, because he is the one we send down to say what we are. You carried a plate down every night for a year and it came back up clean; Touran scraped it into the bin at six every morning for twenty-two years and the year you carried it she did not have to. You slept with him. You priced him. You let him out into the garden at dawn and watched him eat a bird on the lawn, and Touran saw who was on her knees in the grass with feathers on her mouth, and she never turned round again.” He closed the book. “I’m not telling you this to be cruel. I’m telling you because I’m the only one left who can, and because you’ll carry the plate down for whoever buys this house next, and they should at least have one person in it who knows what the plate is for.”

I stood in the room with the light on. I looked at the bed where nobody had slept for twenty-two years until a man who had killed his brother chose it. I looked at the shelf. I thought about the pulse at a hundred and six, and the wrist, and the questions during, and the second door, and the cat, and the sky, and I waited to feel the floor go, and it did not go, because it had never been there.
“Was it difficult?” I said.
“Yes,” said Babak. “Go up, Nasrin. It’s nearly eleven.”
I went up. I set the plate inside the door on my way, because it was still there, and because that is what the plate is for.
At eleven the pipe knocked. Four. A pause. Two. From below, where a living man sat on a dead boy’s bed with a candle and a book.
And from the side — from the party wall, from the back corridor where the old pipes run between the two servants’ quarters — the answer came.
Four. A pause. Two.
I had my knuckle on the iron. I had not decided to. I never do.
Ha.

GLOSSARY
Agha [ah-GHAH] — Sir; the word for the master of a house.
Arghavan [ar-ghah-VAHN] — The Judas tree, which flowers purple across north Tehran in April before its leaves come.
Baba [bah-BAH] — Father. Baba-bozorg [bah-BAH boh-ZORG], grandfather.
Babak [BAH-bak] — The surviving brother; the man in the study.
Baradar [bah-rah-DAR] — Brother.
Behesht-e Zahra [beh-HESHT-eh zah-RAH] — The great cemetery south of Tehran, where the city buries its dead.
Bia payin [bee-YAH pah-YEEN] — Come down. Naya payin, don’t come down.
Chador [chah-DOR] — The full-length cloth a woman wears over her clothes outside.
Chalus road [chah-LOOS] — The mountain highway from Tehran north to the Caspian; narrow, high, and famous for fog and for accidents.
Dokhtaram [dokh-tah-RAM] — “My daughter”; what older women call younger ones, affectionately. Pesaram [peh-sah-RAM], my son.
Door andakhteh [door an-dakh-TEH] — Thrown away, discarded; the word for a thing put in the bin. Zal’s word for the other half of kept.
Elahieh [eh-lah-hee-YEH] — Old-money district in the north of
Tehran, on the slope below the mountains; walled gardens, old plane trees.
Esfand [es-FAND] — Wild rue seed — Peganum harmala

[PEG-ah-num har-MAH-lah] — kept in every Iranian kitchen and burned on coals against the evil eye; it crackles and gives a sweet bitter smoke. Its seeds hold harmine and harmaline, the same substances as the ayahuasca vine; in quantity, a dreaming wakefulness.
Fatemeh [fah-teh-MEH] — The nanny before Nasrin.
Fereshteh [feh-resh-TEH] — “Angel”; the street in Elahieh where the house stands, among the most expensive in the city.
Ha [HAH] — Yes, the short everyday way, said to someone in the next room; baleh [BAH-leh] is the polite one. In Morse, four shorts and a short-long: the nightly knock.
Halva [hal-VAH] — Here, the dark halva made for the dead: flour browned in oil, sugar, rosewater, stirred for an hour and given out in a dead person’s name.
Hamedan [hah-meh-DAHN] — City in the west of Iran, in the mountains; Touran’s village is near it.
Hanooz [hah-NOOZ] — Still.
Hol dadam [hol dah-DAM] — I pushed.
Jigar [jee-GAR] — Literally “liver”; what you call a child you would give your own for. Touran’s name for Zal.
Kandovan tunnel [kan-doh-VAHN] — The high tunnel on the
Chalus road; the bends above it take cars every winter.
Khairat [khey-RAHT] — Food or money given out in a dead person’s name, so that the giving counts for the soul.
Khaneh-ye dar-zan [khah-NEH-yeh dar-ZAN] — “The house that knocks.” The servants’ name for the house.
Khanom [khah-NOM] — Lady, madam; the mistress of a house.
Khazaneh [khah-zah-NEH] — Poor, crowded district in the far south of Tehran, below the railway. Where Nasrin is from.
Khoresh [khoh-RESH] — Stew, served over rice; the ordinary evening meal.
Kont-e Mont Kristo [KONT-eh mont KREES-toh] — The Count of
Monte Cristo; Alexandre Dumas’s novel of 1844, in the old
Persian translation made by the Qajar prince Taher Mirza that lives on the cellar table. Told plainly in the fourth interlude.
Lorestan [loh-res-TAHN] — Mountain province in the west; many of the women who work in the houses of north Tehran come from its villages.
Manteau [man-TOH] — The long coat women wear outside in Iran; the word is French and the garment is required.
Morse code — A code of shorts and longs (dots and dashes) for each letter, made for the telegraph in the 1830s–40s. The brothers use the international table and spell Persian in it by sound.
Nasrin [nas-REEN] — The narrator. A wild rose; the most ordinary name in the city.
Nowruz [now-ROOZ] — The Iranian new year, at the spring equinox in March. The last Thursday before it is the night the whole city goes to the graves.
Nowshahr [now-SHAHR] — Town on the Caspian coast where the family keeps a villa, and where the drowning was said to have happened.
Pishahangi [peesh-ah-han-GEE] — The Iranian Scouts, before the revolution; their manual had the Morse table in it.
Qajar [ghah-JAR] — The dynasty that ruled Iran from the 1790s to
1925; the Persian Monte Cristo was translated in its time.
Rasht [RASHT] — City in the north, about three hours from Tehran over the mountains.
Sabr kon va omidvar bash [SABR kon vah oh-meed-VAR bahsh] —
“Wait and hope”; the last words of the novel, and the ones Zal says most.
Sakht bood? [SAKHT bood] — Was it difficult?
Second door, the — Zal’s name for the barrier he built inside himself at about nine: a bolt on his own side, behind which he put everything he could not have.
Setar [seh-TAR] — The small long-necked Persian lute with four strings, played alone with the nail of the index finger; the instrument of solitary and mystical music. The khanom’s;
Babak’s on Thursdays.
Sholeh zard [sho-LEH zard] — Saffron rice pudding, yellow, made in quantity and given out; what the old man looks at in the refrigerator at three in the morning.
Sizdah Bedar [seez-DAH beh-DAR] — The thirteenth day of the new year, when the whole city goes out to the parks and hills and throws the year’s bad luck into running water; a house is empty that day.
Taher Mirza [TAH-her meer-ZAH] — The Qajar prince who translated The Count of Monte Cristo into Persian in the reign of
Naser al-Din Shah.
Tajrish [taj-REESH] — The square and bazaar at the top of the city, at the foot of the mountains, where the Metro from the south ends.
Tap code — The five-by-five letter grid used by American prisoners in Hanoi from 1965, sent by counting knocks; not the code in this book, but its cousin.
Tarsoo [tar-SOO] — Coward.
Touran [too-RAHN] — The cook; thirty years in the house.
Yasmin [yas-MEEN] — Babak’s daughter, six when the book begins. Jasmine.
Zafaraniyeh [zah-fah-rah-nee-YEH] — Wealthy district next to
Elahieh; where Nasrin’s previous job was.

Zal [ZAHL] — In the Shahnameh [shah-nah-MEH], the old book of kings: the child born with white hair whom his father left on the mountain to die, raised apart from all people by a great bird, who came back pale and strange and wiser than the court. The khanom’s choice of name.
